atoms.title: Equivalence principle
atoms.summary: Locally, gravity and acceleration are indistinguishable — free fall is the closest thing to no force at all.

depths.eli5: Imagine you are in a windowless elevator and the cable snaps, so you and the elevator fall together. While you fall, you float in the middle of the elevator — nothing pushes on you, exactly like an astronaut drifting in empty space far from any planet. The big idea: while you are falling freely, you cannot feel gravity at all. Falling and floating-in-empty-space feel identical from the inside.
depths.core: A 'gravitational field' is the region around a mass where gravity acts; a 'frame' (reference frame) is just the viewpoint of a particular observer, like 'the elevator's point of view.' Einstein noticed that, in a small enough region, the pull of a uniform gravitational field feels exactly the same as being inside an accelerating rocket, and a freely falling viewpoint feels exactly like having no gravity at all. The reason every object falls the same way is that two kinds of mass are equal: inertial mass (how hard it is to push an object into motion) and gravitational mass (how strongly gravity grabs it). Because these are equal to extreme precision, a feather and a hammer fall identically in a vacuum. This lets us stop treating gravity as a force and start treating it as a feature of the viewpoint you choose.
depths.deep: The equality of inertial and gravitational mass is the empirical seed; the principle is only exactly true locally (in a small enough region), because real gravity has tidal effects — neighboring free-fall paths converge, and that convergence is curvature, which cannot be transformed away.

atoms.note: The 'happiest thought of my life' — Einstein, on realizing a falling person feels no weight.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Stand in a windowless elevator. If the cable snaps and you fall freely, you and everything around you drift weightlessly — exactly as an astronaut does in deep space. Now imagine the elevator parked on a rocket accelerating at $9.8\,\text{m/s}^2$ in empty space: you feel pressed to the floor exactly as if you were standing on Earth. **From inside, you cannot tell gravity from acceleration, nor free-fall from floating in empty space.** That single observation is the seed of general relativity.

### Precisely
The **weak equivalence principle** states that the *inertial mass* $m_i$ (the $m$ in $F=m_i a$, resistance to being pushed) equals the *gravitational mass* $m_g$ (the "charge" gravity couples to, the $m$ in $F = m_g g$). Because $m_i = m_g$, the acceleration of a freely falling body, $a = (m_g/m_i)\,g = g$, is **independent of its mass or composition**. The **Einstein equivalence principle** strengthens this: in a small enough region, *all* the laws of physics in a freely falling frame match those of special relativity with no gravity.

### Worked example
Drop a hammer ($1\,\text{kg}$) and a feather ($0.001\,\text{kg}$) in vacuum on the Moon ($g \approx 1.62\,\text{m/s}^2$). Each falls with $a = g = 1.62\,\text{m/s}^2$. From a height of $1.0\,\text{m}$, the time to land is $t = \sqrt{2h/g} = \sqrt{2(1.0)/1.62} \approx 1.11\,\text{s}$ for **both** — Apollo 15 demonstrated exactly this in 1971.

### Why it's true / how it works
Why must they hit together? Because the same number — the body's mass — appears on both sides of $m_g g = m_i a$ and cancels. Newton noticed this cancellation but treated it as a coincidence. Einstein elevated it to a principle: if gravity affects all bodies identically, it is not really a *force* acting on matter but a property of the *spacetime* matter moves through.

### Where it connects
This principle is the doorway to **spacetime-curvature** (gravity = geometry) and to **geodesics** (free-fall = straightest path). The exact local cancellation is why a freely falling **frame** (the **metric** locally reduces to flat Minkowski form) is the natural setting for physics.

### Watch out
The equivalence is only **local**. Over an extended region, real gravity reveals itself through **tidal effects**: two balls dropped side by side toward Earth's center slowly converge, because they fall along lines aiming at the same point. No single accelerating frame can erase that convergence — it is genuine curvature, not a coordinate illusion.

atoms.title: Spacetime curvature
atoms.summary: Gravity is not a force pulling through space — it is the geometry of spacetime being curved by energy.

depths.eli5: Picture a stretchy trampoline. Put a bowling ball in the middle and the surface sags. Now roll a marble nearby and it curves toward the ball — not because the ball reaches out and grabs it, but because the surface itself is bent. Gravity works like that. 'Spacetime' is the combination of the three directions of space plus time, treated as one stretchy fabric. Heavy things bend that fabric, and everything else just coasts along the bends. Earth doesn't tug the Moon with an invisible rope; Earth bends the spacetime around it, and the Moon rolls along the curve.
depths.core: In general relativity (Einstein's theory of gravity), matter and energy curve four-dimensional spacetime, and that curvature tells matter how to move. 'Four-dimensional' just means three space directions plus time. What we feel as gravitational attraction is objects following the straightest available path through a curved geometry — the same way a plane flying 'straight' over the curved Earth traces a curved arc on a flat map. Curvature is detectable in a small region only through tidal effects: the slow relative drift of two nearby objects that are both falling freely. That drift is the un-fakeable fingerprint of real gravity.
depths.deep: Curvature is encoded in the Riemann tensor, which measures the failure of a vector to return to itself after parallel transport around a closed loop; it cannot be removed by any change of coordinates, unlike the apparent 'force' of gravity in a single frame.

atoms.art_prompt: a rubber-sheet grid dimpled by a massive sphere, with a smaller body coasting along the curved gridlines

quiz.prompt: In general relativity, what plays the role that 'gravitational force' played in Newton's picture?
quiz.answer: The curvature of spacetime — matter follows curved geometry rather than being pulled by a force.

quiz.prompt: Explain to a beginner why a single observer in free fall can't detect gravity but tidal forces still reveal it.
quiz.answer: Free fall cancels the uniform part of gravity locally, so you float. But two nearby falling objects drift relative to each other because of curvature — that residual relative acceleration (tidal effect) is the true, un-removable signature of gravity.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Picture a stretched rubber sheet. Place a heavy ball in the middle and the sheet sags into a bowl. Roll a marble past and it curves toward the ball — not because the ball "reaches out," but because the surface it rolls on is bent. Gravity works this way. The Earth does not tug the Moon with an invisible rope; the Earth bends the **spacetime** around it, and the Moon coasts along the bend.

### Precisely
In **general relativity**, gravity *is* the curvature of four-dimensional spacetime (three space dimensions plus time). Matter and energy curve spacetime; the curvature dictates how matter moves. Curvature is quantified by the **Riemann curvature tensor** $R^{\rho}{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}$, built from second derivatives of the **metric** $g_{\mu\nu}$. A region is genuinely curved if and only if $R^{\rho}{}_{\sigma\mu\nu} \neq 0$ — and unlike an apparent "force," this cannot be transformed away by changing coordinates.

### Worked example
Consider geodesic deviation: two test particles a distance $\xi$ apart, both falling freely toward Earth, accelerate toward each other at a relative rate $\ddot{\xi} \sim -\frac{GM}{r^3}\,\xi$. For $r = 6.4\times10^{6}\,\text{m}$ (Earth's radius), $M = 6.0\times10^{24}\,\text{kg}$, two particles $\xi = 10\,\text{m}$ apart converge at about $\frac{(6.67\times10^{-11})(6.0\times10^{24})}{(6.4\times10^{6})^3}\times 10 \approx 1.5\times10^{-5}\,\text{m/s}^2$ — small but nonzero, and that nonzero value is curvature.

### Why it's true / how it works
The rubber-sheet image is a 2D cartoon of a deeper fact: parallel-transporting a vector around a closed loop in curved spacetime returns it rotated. That failure to return unchanged *is* the Riemann tensor. Because tidal convergence cannot be removed in any frame, gravity must be geometry, not a force on top of flat space.

### Where it connects
Curvature is sourced by the **stress-energy** tensor and governed by the **einstein-field-equations**. Free-falling bodies trace **geodesics** through the curved geometry. Light bending in **gravitational-lensing** is curvature acting on photons.

### Watch out
The rubber sheet misleads in two ways: it needs gravity "below" to make the ball sag (circular), and it shows only space, not time. In reality, for slow objects it is the *curvature of time* — not space — that produces most of everyday gravity.

atoms.title: The metric and spacetime intervals
atoms.summary: The metric tensor measures distances and times in spacetime; it is the field that encodes gravity.

depths.eli5: Think of a map where the grid lines are not evenly spaced — in some places the squares are stretched, in others squished. To find the real distance between two dots you can't just count squares; you need a rule that says how much real distance each square is worth at that spot. The metric is exactly that rule. It's a ruler that changes from place to place, and it tells you how far apart two points really are once space is bent.
depths.core: The 'metric tensor,' written g (with two small indices, g_{μν}), is the master rulebook of geometry. A 'tensor' is just an organized table of numbers that behaves correctly when you switch viewpoints. The metric takes the raw difference in coordinates between two nearby points (dx) and turns it into the real physical separation, written ds (the 'interval'). The equation ds² = g_{μν} dx^μ dx^ν is shorthand for 'sum up the coordinate steps, each weighted by the metric, to get the true squared distance.' In flat, gravity-free spacetime the metric is the simple fixed 'Minkowski metric.' In curved spacetime it varies from point to point — and that variation IS gravity. Every geometric thing — lengths, times, angles, and ultimately curvature — is computed from the metric and how it changes.
depths.deep: The interval ds² is invariant under coordinate changes, which is what makes physics observer-independent; the metric's second derivatives build the Riemann curvature, so g_{μν} is simultaneously the 'ruler' and the gravitational potential of general relativity.

quiz.prompt: What does the metric tensor g_{μν} let you compute from coordinate differences?
quiz.answer: Physical spacetime intervals ds — actual distances and proper times — including how they bend in curved spacetime.

quiz.prompt: Why is the invariance of ds² important for physics?
quiz.answer: Because ds² is the same for all observers regardless of coordinates, it guarantees that physical predictions don't depend on the arbitrary coordinate system chosen.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Imagine a map whose grid squares are not all the same size — stretched in some places, squished in others. To find a real distance you cannot just count squares; you need a rule saying how much true distance each square is worth *at that spot*. The **metric** is exactly that rule: a position-dependent ruler.

### Precisely
The metric tensor $g_{\mu\nu}$ converts coordinate differences $dx^\mu$ into the physical squared interval:
$$ds^2 = g_{\mu\nu}\,dx^\mu dx^\nu$$
The indices $\mu,\nu$ run over the four spacetime coordinates $(ct, x, y, z)$, and the repeated-index summation convention is implied. In flat spacetime $g_{\mu\nu}$ is the constant **Minkowski metric** $\eta_{\mu\nu} = \text{diag}(-1,+1,+1,+1)$, giving $ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2$. Units: $ds^2$ has dimensions of length squared (with $c\,dt$ measured in length).

### Worked example
Two events at the same place ($dx=dy=dz=0$) separated by coordinate time $dt$: $ds^2 = -c^2 dt^2$, so the **proper time** is $d\tau = \sqrt{-ds^2}/c = dt$ — a clock at rest just reads coordinate time. Now a light pulse moving along $x$: $0 = -c^2dt^2 + dx^2$ gives $dx/dt = c$. The metric encodes the speed of light automatically.

### Why it's true / how it works
The interval $ds^2$ is **invariant**: every observer, in every coordinate system, computes the same value, even though they disagree on the individual $dt$ and $dx$. This is the relativistic generalization of the Pythagorean theorem — with a crucial minus sign on time that distinguishes past, future, and "elsewhere."

### Where it connects
The metric is the central object of GR: its derivatives build the **Christoffel symbols** in **geodesics**, its second derivatives build curvature in **spacetime-curvature**, and the cosmological metric is the **frw-metric**. Everything — lengths, times, redshifts — is read off $g_{\mu\nu}$.

### Watch out
$ds^2$ can be negative (timelike), zero (null/light), or positive (spacelike) — it is *not* an ordinary positive distance. The sign convention ($-+++$ vs $+---$) varies between books; pick one and stay consistent, because physical predictions do not depend on the choice.

atoms.title: Geodesics — free-fall paths
atoms.summary: Free-falling bodies follow geodesics — the straightest possible paths through curved spacetime.

depths.eli5: On a flat floor the shortest path between two points is a straight line. But on a globe, the 'straightest' path you can walk — a great-circle route, like the arc a long-distance flight follows — looks curved on a flat map. In bent spacetime it's the same: a freely coasting object always takes the locally straightest route available, and because spacetime is curved that route looks like a curve. That's why a thrown ball arcs and why planets loop around the Sun — they're going as straight as the curved geometry allows.
depths.core: A 'geodesic' is the generalization of a straight line to curved spacetime: the path an object follows when nothing but gravity acts on it (no engines, no friction, no push). Technically it 'extremizes proper time' — proper time is the time measured by a clock carried along the path, and a free-falling object travels the route that makes its own clock tick the most. The equation has two parts: the first term (d²x/dτ²) is the path's acceleration as you move along it, and the second term contains the 'Christoffel symbols' (the Γ symbols). The Christoffel symbols are bookkeeping numbers, built from how the metric changes from place to place, that tell you how the direction 'straight ahead' twists as you move through bent space. Setting the whole thing to zero says: 'go straight ahead, correcting only for the bending of the space itself.'
depths.deep: Massive particles follow timelike geodesics (maximizing proper time — the 'twin paradox' resolution), light follows null geodesics; the deviation of neighboring geodesics is governed by the Riemann tensor, directly linking free fall to curvature.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
On a flat floor the straightest path between two points is an ordinary straight line. On a globe, the "straightest" route you can walk — a great circle, like the arc a long flight traces — looks curved on a flat map but is genuinely the straightest path on the sphere. In curved spacetime a freely coasting object always follows the locally straightest available route. Because spacetime is bent, that route looks like an orbit or a falling arc.

### Precisely
A **geodesic** obeys the geodesic equation:
$$\frac{d^2 x^\mu}{d\tau^2} + \Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}\frac{dx^\alpha}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\beta}{d\tau} = 0$$
Here $\tau$ is **proper time** (the clock carried along the path), and the **Christoffel symbols** $\Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta} = \tfrac{1}{2}g^{\mu\nu}(\partial_\alpha g_{\nu\beta} + \partial_\beta g_{\nu\alpha} - \partial_\nu g_{\alpha\beta})$ are built entirely from how the **metric** changes from place to place. The first term is the path's acceleration; the second corrects for the twisting of "straight ahead."

### Worked example
In flat spacetime all $\Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}=0$, so the equation reduces to $d^2x^\mu/d\tau^2 = 0$ — constant velocity, Newton's first law. Near a mass the $\Gamma$ terms are nonzero; solving them for the Sun's field reproduces planetary orbits and predicts Mercury's perihelion advancing an extra $43''$ per century, which Newtonian gravity could not explain.

### Why it's true / how it works
Massive particles follow **timelike** geodesics that *maximize* proper time between two events — a free-falling clock ticks more than any accelerated clock on a nearby path (the resolution of the twin "paradox"). Light follows **null** geodesics with $ds^2 = 0$. Setting the covariant acceleration to zero is the precise statement of "no force but gravity."

### Where it connects
Geodesics realize the **equivalence-principle** (free-fall feels forceless) and the slogan of the **einstein-field-equations** ("spacetime tells matter how to move"). Geodesic *deviation* between neighbors is **spacetime-curvature** in action.

### Watch out
"Straightest" does not mean "shortest" for timelike paths — it means *longest proper time*. And $\Gamma$ is not a tensor: it can be made zero at any single point (a locally free-falling frame), which is the equivalence principle expressed mathematically.

atoms.title: Stress-energy tensor
atoms.summary: The stress-energy tensor packages all energy, momentum, pressure, and stress — it is the source of gravity.

depths.eli5: Newton thought only 'how much stuff' (mass) makes gravity. Einstein found that more things matter: not just mass, but energy, motion, and even pressure all bend spacetime. The stress-energy tensor is a tidy table that lists all of that 'stuff' at every point in space. It's the complete inventory of what gravity responds to.
depths.core: The stress-energy tensor, written T_{μν}, is a 4-by-4 table (a tensor — an organized grid of numbers that switches viewpoints correctly) that records, at every point, the density and flow of energy and momentum. 'Density' means how much per unit volume; 'flux' means how much is flowing through a surface; 'momentum' is mass times velocity, the measure of motion. The top-left entry is energy density (how much energy is packed into each bit of space, and via E=mc² that includes mass). Other entries hold momentum flow and pressure/stress (the push matter exerts sideways and outward). The key surprise of general relativity: gravity is sourced by this entire table, not by mass alone. Because pressure is included, radiation (light, which has pressure but no rest mass) and 'dark energy' (which has large negative pressure) bend spacetime differently from ordinary slow-moving matter ('dust').
depths.deep: Local conservation of energy-momentum, ∇_μ T^{μν} = 0, follows automatically from the field equations via the Bianchi identities — energy conservation is geometrically built in, not imposed.

quiz.prompt: Beyond mass density, what other quantity does the stress-energy tensor include that also gravitates?
quiz.answer: Pressure (and momentum/stress) — which is why radiation and dark energy gravitate differently from ordinary matter.

quiz.prompt: What physical law is automatically encoded in ∇_μ T^{μν} = 0?
quiz.answer: Local conservation of energy and momentum, which follows geometrically from the field equations.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Newton thought only "how much stuff" — mass — creates gravity. Einstein found that energy, momentum, *and pressure* all bend spacetime too. The **stress-energy tensor** is a tidy inventory listing all of that at every point. It is the complete description of what gravity responds to.

### Precisely
The stress-energy tensor $T_{\mu\nu}$ is a symmetric $4\times4$ array. Its component $T^{00}$ is **energy density** (energy per unit volume, including rest-mass energy via $E=mc^2$); $T^{0i}$ are **energy flux / momentum density**; and the spatial block $T^{ij}$ holds **pressure** (on the diagonal) and **shear stress** (off-diagonal). For a **perfect fluid** — the relevant case in cosmology — it simplifies to $T^{\mu\nu} = (\rho + p/c^2)\,u^\mu u^\nu + p\,g^{\mu\nu}$, where $\rho$ is energy density, $p$ is pressure, and $u^\mu$ is the fluid's 4-velocity.

### Worked example
For ordinary cold matter ("dust"), $p \approx 0$, so gravity is sourced essentially by $\rho$ alone — the Newtonian limit. For radiation (a photon gas), $p = \tfrac{1}{3}\rho c^2$: pressure is one-third the energy density, which is why light gravitates differently and why radiation energy density dilutes faster as the universe expands. For **dark-energy**, $p \approx -\rho c^2$: large *negative* pressure, which (counterintuitively) pushes space apart.

### Why it's true / how it works
Local conservation of energy and momentum is written $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu} = 0$. Remarkably, this is not an extra assumption — it follows automatically from the **einstein-field-equations** via the geometric **Bianchi identities**. Conservation is built into the geometry.

### Where it connects
$T_{\mu\nu}$ is the entire right-hand side of the **einstein-field-equations** — the "matter" that tells spacetime how to curve. Its pressure term drives the acceleration equation in the **friedmann-equations** and underlies why **dark-energy** repels.

### Watch out
The most common error is to think only mass density gravitates. In GR, **pressure gravitates too** — and with the *same* sign in the acceleration equation as density. That is precisely why negative-pressure dark energy can reverse cosmic deceleration.

atoms.title: Einstein field equations
atoms.summary: Matter and energy curve spacetime; spacetime curvature tells matter how to move — in one tensor equation.

depths.eli5: This is the single rule at the heart of Einstein's gravity, and it's a two-way street: stuff bends space, and bent space steers stuff. The physicist John Wheeler put it best — 'matter tells spacetime how to curve, and spacetime tells matter how to move.' Everything else in this whole branch is working out the consequences of this one balanced statement.
depths.core: Read the equation as a balance with geometry on the left and contents on the right. The left side has the 'Einstein tensor' G_{μν} — a specific recipe built from spacetime's curvature — so the left side describes the shape of spacetime. The right side has the stress-energy tensor T_{μν} (the inventory of energy, momentum, and pressure from the previous atom), so the right side describes what's filling spacetime. The number out front, 8πG/c⁴, is just a conversion factor (G is Newton's gravitational constant, c is the speed of light) chosen so that in everyday weak, slow situations the equation reproduces Newton's familiar gravity. The extra Λ g_{μν} term is the optional 'cosmological constant' Λ, which behaves like a built-in energy of empty space and becomes important on cosmic scales. So: curvature on the left = matter-and-energy on the right.
depths.deep: These are ten coupled nonlinear partial differential equations; their nonlinearity (gravity gravitates) is why exact solutions are rare and precious — Schwarzschild, Kerr, and the FRW cosmologies are among the few. Λ originally added to permit a static universe, later revived as dark energy.

atoms.note: Λ was Einstein's 'biggest blunder' (his words) — added then removed, then resurrected by the 1998 acceleration discovery.

quiz.prompt: In the Einstein field equations, which side describes geometry and which describes matter?
quiz.answer: The Einstein tensor side (G_{μν} + Λg_{μν}) describes spacetime geometry; the stress-energy side (T_{μν}) describes matter and energy.

quiz.prompt: Summarize the physical meaning of the field equations in one sentence a student can remember.
quiz.answer: Matter and energy tell spacetime how to curve, and the curvature of spacetime tells matter how to move.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
This is the single rule at the heart of gravity, and it is a two-way street: matter bends spacetime, and bent spacetime steers matter. John Wheeler's summary is unbeatable — *"matter tells spacetime how to curve, and spacetime tells matter how to move."* Every result in this branch is a consequence of this one balanced statement.

### Precisely
$$G_{\mu\nu} + \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = \frac{8\pi G}{c^4}\,T_{\mu\nu}$$
The left side is geometry: the **Einstein tensor** $G_{\mu\nu} = R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac{1}{2}R\,g_{\mu\nu}$ (built from curvature) plus the optional **cosmological constant** $\Lambda$ times the **metric**. The right side is contents: the **stress-energy** tensor $T_{\mu\nu}$. The coupling $8\pi G/c^4 \approx 2.1\times10^{-43}\,\text{s}^2\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-1}$ is fixed by demanding agreement with Newtonian gravity in the weak, slow limit.

### Worked example
In the weak-field, low-speed limit, the time-time component reduces to Poisson's equation $\nabla^2 \Phi = 4\pi G \rho$, exactly Newtonian gravity — confirming the constant out front. The smallness of $8\pi G/c^4$ ($c^4$ is enormous) is why colossal mass is needed to curve spacetime appreciably: the Sun deflects starlight by only $1.75''$.

### Why it's true / how it works
The equations are *ten coupled nonlinear* partial differential equations (the symmetric $4\times4$ tensors each have ten independent components). The nonlinearity means **gravity gravitates** — gravitational energy itself bends spacetime — which is why exact solutions are rare and precious: Schwarzschild (black holes), Kerr (spinning), and the **frw-metric** (cosmology).

### Where it connects
Feeding the **frw-metric** into these equations yields the **friedmann-equations** that govern cosmic expansion. The $\Lambda$ term reappears as **cosmological-constant** dark energy.

### Watch out
$\Lambda$ was famously Einstein's "biggest blunder" — he added it to force a static universe, dropped it after Hubble found expansion, and it was resurrected in 1998 to explain **dark-energy**. Do not read the equation as "force = mass"; both sides are tensors describing geometry and content, not a Newtonian force law.

atoms.title: Cosmological principle
atoms.summary: On large enough scales the universe is homogeneous and isotropic — the same everywhere and in every direction.

depths.eli5: Up close the universe is lumpy — planets here, empty gaps there. But zoom way out, past individual galaxies, and the lumps blur into an even haze that looks the same no matter where you're standing or which direction you look. There's no center of the universe and no edge you could point to, and no special direction that's different from the rest.
depths.core: The cosmological principle is the starting assumption of modern cosmology. It says that, once you average over enormous distances (hundreds of millions of light-years — a light-year is the distance light travels in a year), the universe is 'homogeneous' (the same at every location, no special spot) and 'isotropic' (the same in every direction, no special way to point). These two symmetries are an enormous simplification: they let cosmologists shrink Einstein's ten complicated field equations down to just a couple of equations describing a single number, the 'scale factor,' that captures the whole large-scale universe. It's an idealization — locally the universe is very lumpy — but on the largest scales the evidence backs it up.
depths.deep: It is an idealization that holds statistically on large scales — galaxies cluster strongly on small scales, but the CMB's near-perfect uniformity (~1 part in 100,000) is the strongest observational support for large-scale isotropy around us.

quiz.answer: Homogeneity (same at every location) and isotropy (same in every direction) on large scales.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Up close the universe is lumpy — planets here, voids there. But zoom out past individual galaxies and the lumps blur into an even haze that looks the same wherever you stand and whichever way you look. There is no center, no edge, no special direction. This is the working assumption that makes cosmology tractable.

### Precisely
The **cosmological principle** asserts that, averaged over sufficiently large scales (roughly $\gtrsim 100\,\text{Mpc} \approx 300$ million light-years), the universe is:
- **homogeneous** — the same at every *location* (no privileged place), and
- **isotropic** — the same in every *direction* (no privileged direction).

Homogeneity and isotropy about every point together force a very restrictive geometry — exactly the **frw-metric**, with only three allowed spatial curvatures (flat, spherical, hyperbolic).

### Worked example
The **cmb-origin** is uniform across the whole sky to about 1 part in $10^5$ after removing the dipole from our own motion. If the universe had a center, an observer off-center would see a hotter CMB on one side and cooler on the other — a large-scale anisotropy that is simply not present. That near-perfect uniformity is the strongest direct evidence for isotropy around us.

### Why it's true / how it works
Isotropy is *observed* (the CMB, galaxy counts, radio sources). Homogeneity is then inferred: if the universe is isotropic about us *and* we are not special (the Copernican principle), it must be isotropic about every point — and isotropy about every point mathematically implies homogeneity.

### Where it connects
It is the symmetry assumption that collapses Einstein's ten **einstein-field-equations** into the two simple **friedmann-equations** for a single function, the **scale-factor**. Galaxy **large-scale-structure** and **redshift-surveys** test how well it holds.

### Watch out
It is a statement about *large-scale averages*, not local reality — galaxies cluster strongly on small scales. And it is an assumption supported by evidence, not a theorem: the "end of greatness" scale beyond which the universe looks smooth is itself an active research question.

atoms.title: FRW metric
atoms.summary: The unique metric of a homogeneous, isotropic universe — flat, open, or closed, all scaled by a(t).

depths.eli5: Once you assume the universe looks the same everywhere and in every direction, its shape gets incredibly simple to describe: just one stretchy number, written a(t), that says how big everything is at time t, plus a single choice of overall shape — flat like a tabletop, curved-closed like the surface of a ball, or curved-open like a saddle. This metric is that description boiled down to its essentials.
depths.core: The FRW metric (Friedmann–Robertson–Walker, sometimes FLRW with Lemaître's name added) is the unique shape the metric must take once you accept the cosmological principle. Reading the equation: −c²dt² is the time part (c is the speed of light, t is time), and the bracket is the space part. The 'curvature constant' k labels which of three uniform spatial shapes you have: k = +1 is 'closed' (finite, ball-like), k = 0 is 'flat' (the everyday geometry where parallel lines stay parallel), and k = −1 is 'open' (infinite, saddle-like). The function a(t), the 'scale factor,' multiplies every spatial distance and grows over time — that growth is the expansion of the universe. 't' here is 'cosmic time,' the time read by clocks moving along with the average flow of matter.
depths.deep: The coordinates are comoving: galaxies sit at fixed (r, θ, φ) while a(t) stretches the physical distances between them. Observations strongly favor k ≈ 0 (spatially flat) to within current measurement error.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Once you accept that the universe looks the same everywhere and in every direction, its geometry becomes astonishingly simple to write down: one stretching number $a(t)$ that says how big everything is at time $t$, plus a single choice of overall shape — flat like a tabletop, closed like a sphere's surface, or open like a saddle. The FRW metric *is* that description, distilled.

### Precisely
$$ds^2 = -c^2\,dt^2 + a(t)^2\!\left[\frac{dr^2}{1 - k r^2} + r^2\,d\Omega^2\right]$$
where $d\Omega^2 = d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2$. Here $t$ is **cosmic time** (read by clocks comoving with matter), $(r,\theta,\phi)$ are **comoving** coordinates, $a(t)$ is the dimensionless **scale-factor**, and $k$ is the curvature constant: $k=+1$ closed (finite, sphere-like), $k=0$ flat, $k=-1$ open (infinite, saddle-like).

### Worked example
For a flat universe ($k=0$), the spatial part is just $a(t)^2(dr^2 + r^2 d\Omega^2)$ — ordinary Euclidean space scaled by $a(t)$. Two galaxies at comoving separation $\Delta r$ have physical distance $D(t) = a(t)\,\Delta r$. If $a$ doubles, $D$ doubles, while $\Delta r$ stays fixed — the galaxies never "move" in comoving coordinates; space itself stretches.

### Why it's true / how it works
The cosmological principle (homogeneity + isotropy about every point) is so restrictive that it *uniquely* fixes the metric to this form up to the three values of $k$ and the free function $a(t)$. All the physics then lives in determining how $a(t)$ evolves — which the **friedmann-equations** supply.

### Where it connects
This metric, plugged into the **einstein-field-equations**, yields the **friedmann-equations**. The factor $a(t)$ drives **cosmological-redshift** ($1+z = 1/a$) and **hubble-law**. Observations (CMB **acoustic-peaks**) favor $k \approx 0$.

### Watch out
$r$ here is a *comoving* coordinate, not a physical distance — physical distance is $a(t)$ times an integral over $r$. Also, $k=0$ "flat" refers to *spatial* flatness; the full 4D spacetime is still curved (it is expanding).

atoms.title: Scale factor a(t)
atoms.summary: A single function a(t) sets the size of the universe; its growth is cosmic expansion.

depths.core: The scale factor a(t) is a single number, changing with time t, that tracks how stretched-out the universe is. The distance between any two 'comoving' objects — objects just drifting along with the overall expansion, not zooming around on their own — scales in proportion to a(t): if a was 1/2 in the past, all those distances were half as big then. Because everything large-scale rides on this one number, the history of the universe is essentially the story of how a(t) grows. Its rate of change (first derivative, written ȧ) is the expansion speed, and the rate of change of that (second derivative) says whether the expansion is speeding up or slowing down. The word 'derivative' just means 'how fast something is changing.'
depths.deep: a(t) is dimensionless with the convention a(t₀)=1; redshift, temperature, and density all map directly onto it (1+z = 1/a), making a(t) the master clock of cosmic history even though it is not directly observable — only ratios are.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Draw galaxies as dots on a balloon and inflate it. Every dot recedes from every other, yet no dot is the center. The **scale factor** $a(t)$ is essentially "how inflated the balloon is at time $t$." When $a$ doubles, every distance between dots doubles — but the dots (galaxies) themselves do not grow.

### Precisely
$a(t)$ is a dimensionless function of **cosmic time**, normalized so that today $a(t_0) = 1$. The physical distance between two comoving objects scales as $D(t) = a(t)\,D_0$, where $D_0$ is today's distance. Its first derivative $\dot a = da/dt$ measures the expansion rate; the **Hubble parameter** is $H \equiv \dot a / a$. The second derivative $\ddot a$ tells whether expansion is accelerating ($\ddot a > 0$) or decelerating ($\ddot a < 0$).

### Worked example
If at some past epoch $a = 0.25$, then all comoving distances were one-quarter of today's, the universe's volume was $0.25^3 \approx 0.016$ of today's (about 64 times denser in matter, since $\rho_m \propto a^{-3}$), and the **cosmological-redshift** of light emitted then is $1+z = 1/a = 4$, i.e. $z=3$.

### Why it's true / how it works
$a(t)$ is the *only* free function the **cosmological-principle** allows in the **frw-metric**. Every large-scale quantity rides on it: density $\rho_m \propto a^{-3}$, radiation $\rho_r \propto a^{-4}$, temperature $T \propto a^{-1}$, redshift $1+z = 1/a$. It is the master clock of cosmic history.

### Where it connects
Its evolution is set by the **friedmann-equations**; its growth rate is **hubble-law**; its inverse is **cosmological-redshift**; its first instant is reshaped by **inflation**.

### Watch out
$a(t)$ itself is *not directly observable* — only *ratios* are, because its present value is a convention ($a(t_0)=1$). What we actually measure is redshift $z$, then infer $a$. Also, individual galaxies and atoms are *not* stretched by $a$ — bound systems decouple from the expansion.

atoms.title: Cosmological redshift
atoms.summary: Expansion stretches light's wavelength as it travels — distant galaxies look redder by exactly the factor space has grown.

depths.eli5: Light travels as waves, and the color you see depends on the wave's length — shorter waves look bluer, longer waves look redder. Draw a wave on a rubber band, then stretch the band: the wave gets longer. As the universe grows, it stretches the light waves crossing it the same way, making them longer and therefore redder. So light from very distant galaxies, which spent a long time crossing growing space, arrives shifted toward red. That shift is called 'redshift.'
depths.core: A 'photon' is a single particle of light, and its 'wavelength' is the length of one wave. As a photon crosses expanding space, its wavelength stretches in exact proportion to the scale factor a(t). 'Redshift' z is the fractional amount the wavelength grew: the formula 1 + z = λ_observed / λ_emitted = 1 / a(t_emit) says the stretch factor equals one over the scale factor at the moment the light left (t_emit). So measuring a galaxy's redshift directly tells you how small the universe was when its light departed. Important subtlety: this is NOT the everyday 'Doppler shift' you hear when a siren passes (caused by something moving through space). Cosmological redshift comes from space itself stretching while the light is in flight.
depths.deep: Distinguishing cosmological redshift from peculiar-velocity Doppler shifts matters near home; at high z the relation 1+z=1/a is exact within FRW and is how we read the scale factor off the spectrum of any source — redshift is our primary cosmic distance/time coordinate.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Light is a wave, and color depends on its wavelength — shorter looks bluer, longer looks redder. Draw a wave on a rubber band and stretch the band: the wave lengthens. As the universe grows, it stretches the light waves crossing it, lengthening them and shifting them toward red. Distant galaxies, whose light spent eons crossing growing space, arrive visibly reddened.

### Precisely
$$1 + z = \frac{\lambda_{\text{obs}}}{\lambda_{\text{emit}}} = \frac{1}{a(t_{\text{emit}})}$$
The **redshift** $z$ is the fractional increase in wavelength: $z = (\lambda_{\text{obs}} - \lambda_{\text{emit}})/\lambda_{\text{emit}}$. Because $a(t_0)=1$ today, the stretch factor equals exactly $1/a$ at the moment of emission. Measuring $z$ therefore directly reads off how small the universe was when the light departed.

### Worked example
A galaxy shows a spectral line at observed wavelength $\lambda_{\text{obs}} = 820\,\text{nm}$ that is known to be emitted at $\lambda_{\text{emit}} = 656\,\text{nm}$ (hydrogen-alpha). Then $1+z = 820/656 = 1.25$, so $z = 0.25$, and $a(t_{\text{emit}}) = 1/1.25 = 0.80$ — the universe was 80% of its present size when that light left. The **cmb-origin** has $z \approx 1100$, so $a \approx 1/1101 \approx 0.0009$.

### Why it's true / how it works
A photon's wavelength is carried along with the expanding space it travels through; the comoving wavelength is fixed, so the physical wavelength scales as $a(t)$. This is a property of waves propagating through the **frw-metric**, derived directly from null **geodesics**.

### Where it connects
Redshift is the master observable of cosmology: it sets the **scale-factor** at emission, drives **thermal-history** ($T \propto 1+z$), and is the depth coordinate in **redshift-surveys** and the **hubble-law**.

### Watch out
Cosmological redshift is **not** an ordinary Doppler shift from motion *through* space — it comes from space itself stretching while the light is in flight. Near home, peculiar-velocity Doppler shifts contaminate the measurement; at high $z$ the relation $1+z = 1/a$ is exact within FRW.

atoms.title: Hubble–Lemaître law
atoms.summary: Galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance — the observational signature of cosmic expansion.

depths.eli5: When astronomers measure how fast galaxies are moving away from us, they find a clean pattern: a galaxy twice as far away is moving away twice as fast. That's exactly what you'd see if the whole of space were quietly growing everywhere at once — and it's the everyday evidence that the universe is expanding.
depths.core: 'Recession velocity' is how fast a galaxy moves away from us. The Hubble–Lemaître law says this velocity v is simply proportional to the galaxy's distance d: v = H₀ d. The proportionality number H₀ is the 'Hubble constant,' about 70 km/s per megaparsec today (a megaparsec, Mpc, is about 3.26 million light-years; the units mean a galaxy gains ~70 km/s of recession for every Mpc of distance). This doesn't mean we sit at a center — in a uniformly expanding universe every observer sees the same law. The broader 'Hubble parameter' H = ȧ/a is the fractional growth rate of the scale factor (ȧ is how fast a is changing, divided by a itself), and its present value H₀ roughly sets both the age and the size scale of the universe.
depths.deep: 1/H₀ is the Hubble time (~14 billion years), a first estimate of the age; the law is exact only at low z, where v ≈ cz — at high z one must use the full FRW relation between redshift and distance rather than a naive velocity.

atoms.note: Renamed Hubble–Lemaître law in 2018 to credit Lemaître's 1927 derivation.

quiz.answer: It relates a galaxy's recession velocity to its distance (v = H₀d), with H₀ ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc.

quiz.prompt: Show why 1/H₀ gives a rough age of the universe.
quiz.answer: If expansion had been at a constant rate, a galaxy at distance d receding at v = H₀d took time d/v = 1/H₀ to get there; 1/H₀ ≈ 14 Gyr is therefore a first estimate of the age.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
When astronomers measure how fast galaxies recede, a clean pattern emerges: a galaxy twice as far away moves away twice as fast. That is exactly what you would see if *all of space* were quietly growing everywhere at once — the everyday signature of an expanding universe, and historically the discovery that launched modern cosmology.

### Precisely
$$v = H_0\,d, \qquad H \equiv \frac{\dot a}{a}$$
$v$ is recession velocity, $d$ is distance, and $H_0$ is the **Hubble constant** — the present value of the **Hubble parameter** $H = \dot a/a$, the fractional growth rate of the **scale-factor**. Measured value: $H_0 \approx 70\,\text{km/s/Mpc}$, where $1\,\text{Mpc} \approx 3.26$ million light-years $\approx 3.09\times10^{19}\,\text{km}$. So a galaxy gains $\sim70\,\text{km/s}$ of recession per megaparsec of distance.

### Worked example
A galaxy $100\,\text{Mpc}$ away recedes at $v = 70 \times 100 = 7000\,\text{km/s}$. The **Hubble time** $t_H = 1/H_0$ gives a rough age: converting, $1/H_0 = (3.09\times10^{19}\,\text{km})/(70\,\text{km/s}) \approx 4.4\times10^{17}\,\text{s} \approx 14$ billion years — close to the true $13.8\,\text{Gyr}$.

### Why it's true / how it works
In a uniformly expanding **frw-metric**, physical distance is $d = a(t)\,d_{\text{comoving}}$, so $\dot d = \dot a\,d_{\text{comoving}} = (\dot a/a)\,d = H d$. The proportionality is automatic and *centerless*: every comoving observer sees the same law, so our seeing recession everywhere does not put us at the middle.

### Where it connects
$H_0$ sets the age and size scale of the cosmos and anchors the **cosmic-distance-ladder**. Its precise value is the subject of the **hubble-tension**. $H(t)$ appears throughout the **friedmann-equations** and **critical-density**.

### Watch out
$v = H_0 d$ is exact only at *low* redshift, where $v \approx cz$. At high $z$, naive "velocity" exceeds $c$ for very distant galaxies — which is *not* a violation, because cosmological recession is the stretching of space, not motion through it. Use the full FRW distance–redshift relation there.

atoms.title: Friedmann equations
atoms.summary: The Einstein equations applied to a uniform universe — they govern how the scale factor evolves.

depths.eli5: This is the universe's growth equation. Tell it what the universe is made of right now — ordinary matter, radiation (light), its overall shape, and dark energy — and it tells you how fast the universe is growing and whether that growth is speeding up or slowing down. It's the master equation of cosmology.
depths.core: When you feed the simple FRW shape of the universe into Einstein's field equations, all that machinery collapses into the much friendlier Friedmann equations. The one shown gives H², the square of the expansion rate (H = ȧ/a, the fractional growth rate from the Hubble-law atom). On the right: ρ (Greek 'rho') is the total energy density — how much energy-and-matter is packed into each bit of space; the −kc²/a² term carries the universe's curvature k (its overall shape); and the Λ term is dark energy. A companion 'acceleration' equation shows that pressure, not just density, decides whether expansion speeds up or slows down. The key plot twist: the different ingredients thin out at different rates as the universe grows, so each one takes its turn dominating the cosmic story.
depths.deep: Matter density scales as a⁻³, radiation as a⁻⁴ (extra factor from redshift), curvature as a⁻², and Λ stays constant — so the universe passes through radiation-, matter-, and Λ-dominated eras as a grows, with a(t)∝t^{1/2}, t^{2/3}, and e^{Ht} respectively.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
This is the universe's growth equation. Tell it what the cosmos is made of right now — matter, radiation, curvature, dark energy — and it tells you how fast the universe expands and whether that expansion speeds up or slows down. Everything about cosmic history follows from integrating it.

### Precisely
The first Friedmann equation, from plugging the **frw-metric** into the **einstein-field-equations**:
$$\left(\frac{\dot a}{a}\right)^2 = H^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - \frac{k c^2}{a^2} + \frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}$$
$\rho$ is total energy density, $k$ the curvature constant, $\Lambda$ the **cosmological-constant**. A companion **acceleration equation** $\ddot a/a = -\frac{4\pi G}{3}(\rho + 3p/c^2) + \frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}$ shows that *pressure* $p$, not just density, decides acceleration.

### Worked example
In a flat ($k=0$), matter-only universe with $\Lambda=0$: solving $H^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho$ with $\rho \propto a^{-3}$ yields $a(t) \propto t^{2/3}$. Then $H = \dot a/a = \frac{2}{3t}$, so the age is $t_0 = \frac{2}{3 H_0}$ — about $9.3\,\text{Gyr}$ for $H_0=70$, notably *younger* than the real universe, which is one early hint that matter alone is not the whole story.

### Why it's true / how it works
Each ingredient dilutes differently as $a$ grows: matter $\rho_m \propto a^{-3}$ (volume), radiation $\rho_r \propto a^{-4}$ (volume *plus* one redshift factor per photon), curvature $\propto a^{-2}$, and $\Lambda$ stays constant. So the universe passes through **radiation-dominated** ($a \propto t^{1/2}$), **matter-dominated** ($a \propto t^{2/3}$), and **$\Lambda$-dominated** ($a \propto e^{Ht}$) eras in turn.

### Where it connects
These equations underpin **critical-density**, the **big-bang**, **dark-energy**, and the whole **lambda-cdm** model. The acceleration equation is what **dark-energy** exploits.

### Watch out
The acceleration depends on $\rho + 3p/c^2$: a component with strongly negative pressure ($p < -\rho c^2/3$) makes $\ddot a > 0$. Forgetting the pressure term is the classic mistake that makes cosmic acceleration seem impossible.

atoms.title: Critical density and Ω
atoms.summary: The density that makes space exactly flat; Ω compares the actual density to it and fixes the geometry.

depths.eli5: There's one special amount of stuff that makes the universe come out perfectly flat — like a tabletop, where parallel lines stay parallel forever. Pack in more than that special amount and space curves around on itself like the surface of a ball; pack in less and it curves the other way like a saddle. Measuring how much stuff the universe actually has tells you which shape we live in.
depths.core: Take the Friedmann equation and ask: what energy density would make the curvature term k vanish, giving a perfectly flat universe? That special value is the 'critical density,' ρ_c = 3H²/(8πG), where H is the expansion rate and G is Newton's gravitational constant. Now compare the real density ρ to this critical value: the ratio Ω = ρ/ρ_c (Greek capital 'Omega') is the 'density parameter,' and it fixes the geometry. Ω > 1 means denser than critical → space is closed and curves like a ball; Ω = 1 means exactly critical → space is flat; Ω < 1 means underdense → space is open and saddle-shaped. When you add up Ω from every ingredient — ordinary matter, radiation, and dark energy — observations land remarkably close to a total of 1, meaning the universe is flat.
depths.deep: The sum Ω_m + Ω_r + Ω_Λ + Ω_k = 1 is an identity, so 'flatness' (Ω_k ≈ 0) is the measured statement that the energy components add to the critical density to within ~0.5% — a result inflation predicts and the CMB confirms.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
There is one special amount of "stuff" that makes the universe come out perfectly flat — tabletop geometry, where parallel lines stay parallel forever. Pack in more and space curves closed like a sphere; pack in less and it curves open like a saddle. Measuring how much the universe actually contains tells you which shape we inhabit.

### Precisely
$$\rho_c = \frac{3 H^2}{8\pi G}, \qquad \Omega \equiv \frac{\rho}{\rho_c}$$
$\rho_c$ is the **critical density** — the value that makes the curvature term $k=0$ in the **friedmann-equations**. $\Omega$, the **density parameter**, compares actual density to critical. $\Omega > 1 \Rightarrow$ closed ($k=+1$); $\Omega = 1 \Rightarrow$ flat ($k=0$); $\Omega < 1 \Rightarrow$ open ($k=-1$).

### Worked example
Today $H_0 \approx 70\,\text{km/s/Mpc} = 2.27\times10^{-18}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. Then
$$\rho_c = \frac{3 (2.27\times10^{-18})^2}{8\pi (6.67\times10^{-11})} \approx 9.2\times10^{-27}\,\text{kg/m}^3,$$
about **5–6 hydrogen atoms per cubic meter** — an astonishingly sparse density that nonetheless dictates the geometry of the whole cosmos.

### Why it's true / how it works
Rearranging the first Friedmann equation gives the identity $\Omega_m + \Omega_r + \Omega_\Lambda + \Omega_k = 1$, where $\Omega_k \equiv -kc^2/(a^2H^2)$ encodes curvature. "Flatness" is the *measured* statement that the energy components sum to the critical density, i.e. $\Omega_k \approx 0$.

### Where it connects
Observations give $\Omega_m \approx 0.31$, $\Omega_\Lambda \approx 0.69$, radiation negligible — summing to $\approx 1.00$, so $\Omega_k \approx 0$ to within $\sim0.5\%$. This near-perfect flatness is predicted by **inflation** and confirmed by the **acoustic-peaks**, and it feeds directly into **lambda-cdm**.

### Watch out
$\rho_c$ is *not* a fixed constant — it depends on $H$, which changes with time, so $\rho_c$ was much higher in the past. And $\Omega=1$ does not mean the universe will halt; fate depends on *which* components supply the density, especially **dark-energy**.

atoms.title: The Big Bang — a hot dense beginning
atoms.summary: Run the expansion backward and the universe was hotter, denser, and smaller — the Big Bang is that hot early state.

depths.eli5: Play the movie of the expanding universe backwards. Everything that is flying apart today was packed closer and closer together the further back you go — and packing things tightly together makes them hot (squeeze any gas and it heats up). So long ago the whole universe was tiny, dense, and blazing hot. That hot, tiny early state is what 'the Big Bang' means. It was NOT an explosion that went off at one spot in empty space — it was the entire universe starting out small and hot everywhere at once.
depths.core: The Big Bang is the name for the early, hot, dense phase of the universe, back when the scale factor a(t) was tiny. As a grew, the universe cooled and thinned out ('rarefied'). The model rests on three independent pillars of evidence that all point to the same hot dense origin roughly 13.8 billion years ago: (1) the observed expansion of the universe (galaxies flying apart, the Hubble law); (2) the cosmic microwave background, a faint glow of leftover heat filling the whole sky; and (3) the measured amounts of the lightest chemical elements (hydrogen, helium), which match what a hot early furnace would have produced. A common misconception worth deleting: there is no center and no edge — space itself expanded everywhere, not stuff blasting outward into a pre-existing void.
depths.deep: Extrapolating a → 0 gives a formal singularity of infinite density, but that is a breakdown of classical general relativity, not a verified physical event — the earliest moments require quantum gravity, and the standard hot Big Bang is only confidently described from roughly a microsecond onward.

atoms.note: The age 13.8 Gyr comes from fitting the expansion history (CMB + supernovae + large-scale structure).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Play the movie of the expanding universe backwards. Everything flying apart today was packed closer the further back you go — and squeezing matter together heats it (compress any gas and it warms). So long ago the whole universe was tiny, dense, and blazing hot. That hot early state *is* the Big Bang. Crucially, it was **not** an explosion at one spot in pre-existing space — it was the entire universe starting small and hot *everywhere at once*.

### Precisely
The **Big Bang** is the hot, dense early phase when the **scale-factor** $a(t)$ was small. As $a$ grew, the universe cooled ($T \propto 1/a$) and thinned. The model rests on **three independent pillars**: (1) the observed **hubble-law** expansion; (2) the **cmb-origin** relic glow; (3) the measured **bbn** light-element abundances. All three point to an origin about $13.8$ billion years ago.

### Worked example
Estimate the age crudely from the **hubble-law**: $t \sim 1/H_0 \approx 14\,\text{Gyr}$. A more careful integration of the **friedmann-equations** with $\Omega_m \approx 0.31$, $\Omega_\Lambda \approx 0.69$ yields $t_0 = 13.8\,\text{Gyr}$ — and the independent **cmb-origin** fit agrees, a powerful consistency check.

### Why it's true / how it works
Extrapolating $a \to 0$ makes density and temperature formally infinite — a *singularity*. But that is a breakdown of classical GR, not a verified event: the earliest instants need quantum gravity. The standard hot Big Bang is confidently described only from roughly a microsecond onward, where known physics applies and predictions (like **bbn**) match data.

### Where it connects
It frames the entire cosmic-history sequence: **inflation**, **baryogenesis**, **bbn**, **recombination**, **cmb-origin**, structure formation, and **dark-energy** domination — synthesized in **cosmic-history-synthesis**.

### Watch out
The deepest misconception: the Big Bang was *not* matter blasting outward into empty space. There is **no center and no edge**. Space itself expanded uniformly. Asking "where did it happen?" is like asking which point on a balloon's surface the inflation started from — every point did.

atoms.title: Thermal history and temperature scaling
atoms.summary: The universe cools as it expands; its temperature is inversely proportional to the scale factor.

depths.eli5: Letting a gas expand cools it down — it's why an aerosol can feels cold as it sprays. The universe does the same thing as it grows: it cools, and in a beautifully simple way. Make the universe twice as big and its temperature drops to half. So the early, tiny universe was scorching, and it has been cooling ever since.
depths.core: Temperature, written T, measures how hot something is (here in kelvin, K, the science temperature scale starting from absolute zero). Because the universe is bathed in light whose wavelengths stretch as the scale factor a grows, the temperature of that cosmic radiation falls in lockstep: T ∝ 1/a, which equals 1 + z (the redshift). This one relation turns the scale factor into a cosmic thermometer — each chapter of history happened at a characteristic temperature: light-element formation at about a billion kelvin (10⁹ K), atoms forming at about 3000 K, and the leftover glow we see today at just 2.725 K. So 'how hot was the universe then?' and 'how big was it then?' are the same question.
depths.deep: The scaling is exact for a thermal blackbody spectrum, which expansion preserves: a redshifted blackbody is still a blackbody at lower temperature — the reason the CMB remains a near-perfect Planck spectrum despite stretching by a factor of ~1100.

quiz.prompt: How does the temperature of the cosmic radiation scale with the scale factor?

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Let a gas expand and it cools — the reason an aerosol can feels cold while spraying. The universe does the same as it grows: it cools, and beautifully simply. Make the universe twice as big and its temperature halves. So the early, tiny universe was scorching, and it has been cooling ever since.

### Precisely
$$T \propto \frac{1}{a} = 1 + z$$
$T$ is the temperature (in kelvin, K) of the cosmic radiation bath. Because photon wavelengths stretch with the **scale-factor** ($\lambda \propto a$) and a blackbody's temperature scales inversely with wavelength, $T \propto 1/a$, which equals $1+z$ via the **cosmological-redshift** relation. This turns $a$ into a cosmic thermometer.

### Worked example
Today $T_0 = 2.725\,\text{K}$. At **recombination**, $z \approx 1100$, so $T = 2.725 \times (1+1100) = 2.725 \times 1101 \approx 3000\,\text{K}$ — exactly hot enough to keep hydrogen ionized until just below this. At **bbn**, $z \approx 4\times10^{8}$, so $T \approx 2.725 \times 4\times10^{8} \approx 10^{9}\,\text{K}$ — the billion-degree furnace that forged helium.

### Why it's true / how it works
The scaling is *exact* for a thermal **blackbody** spectrum, because expansion preserves the blackbody form: a redshifted blackbody at temperature $T$ becomes a blackbody at lower temperature $T/(1+z)$, with every wavelength stretched by the same factor. This is precisely why the **cmb-origin**, stretched by a factor $\sim1100$, remains a near-perfect Planck spectrum today.

### Where it connects
This relation pins every epoch to a temperature: **bbn** ($\sim10^9\,\text{K}$), **recombination** ($\sim3000\,\text{K}$), today ($2.725\,\text{K}$). "How hot was it then?" and "how big was it then?" are the same question. It governs **baryogenesis** timing and the radiation era of the **friedmann-equations**.

### Watch out
The simple $T \propto 1/a$ holds for radiation that freely expands; it gets small corrections when relativistic particle species annihilate (e.g. electron–positron annihilation heats photons relative to neutrinos), which is why the neutrino background is slightly cooler ($\sim1.95\,\text{K}$) than the photon CMB.

atoms.title: Cosmic inflation
atoms.summary: A burst of exponential expansion in the first instant explains the universe's flatness, uniformity, and seed fluctuations.

depths.eli5: In the first sliver of a second after the Big Bang, the universe is thought to have ballooned in size by a staggering amount almost instantly. Think of a wrinkled balloon blown up so fast that any wrinkle gets stretched flat and smooth. That sudden growth smoothed the universe out, flattened its shape, and stretched microscopic jitters into the faint lumps that would later grow into galaxies.
depths.core: Inflation is the idea that the very early universe went through a brief burst of runaway expansion — the size grew exponentially, a ∝ e^{Ht} (e is the natural growth constant; H sets the breakneck rate). The proposed engine is a 'scalar field,' a kind of energy spread evenly through space whose stored ('potential') energy temporarily acts like powerful anti-gravity. Inflation was invented to fix two puzzles in the plain Big Bang: the 'horizon problem' (why regions on opposite sides of the sky have the same temperature even though, without inflation, they were never close enough to swap heat) and the 'flatness problem' (why the density parameter Ω is so suspiciously close to 1). Both are solved if a tiny patch that WAS in contact got stretched to cover the entire visible universe. As a bonus, tiny quantum jitters (unavoidable random fluctuations at microscopic scales) got stretched to cosmic size and became the seeds from which all galaxies grew.
depths.deep: Inflation's most testable prediction is a nearly scale-invariant spectrum of adiabatic, Gaussian density perturbations with slight red tilt (n_s ≈ 0.965) — confirmed by the CMB; a primordial gravitational-wave (B-mode) signal would be smoking-gun evidence but has not yet been detected.

atoms.note: Proposed by Guth (1980) and refined by Linde, Albrecht, and Steinhardt.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
In the first sliver of a second after the Big Bang, the universe is thought to have ballooned in size by a staggering factor almost instantly. Imagine a wrinkled balloon blown up so violently that any wrinkle is stretched flat and smooth. That sudden growth smoothed the universe, flattened its geometry, and stretched microscopic quantum jitters into the faint lumps that later grew into galaxies.

### Precisely
**Inflation** is a brief epoch of accelerated expansion, $a(t) \propto e^{Ht}$, driven by a **scalar field** (the "inflaton") whose potential energy temporarily acts like a large **cosmological-constant**. During inflation $\ddot a > 0$ for a stretch lasting at least $N \gtrsim 60$ **e-folds** (factors of $e$ in $a$), i.e. growth by at least $e^{60} \approx 10^{26}$.

### Worked example
A patch needs $\sim60$ e-folds to solve the puzzles. If inflation ran at $H \sim 10^{36}\,\text{s}^{-1}$, then $60$ e-folds take $t = N/H \approx 60/10^{36} = 6\times10^{-35}\,\text{s}$ — over in a tiny fraction of a fraction of a second, yet stretching a sub-atomic patch to larger than the entire observable universe.

### Why it's true / how it works
Inflation was invented to cure two puzzles of the plain Big Bang. The **horizon problem**: regions on opposite sides of the sky share the same CMB temperature despite never being in causal contact — solved if they *were* in contact in a tiny pre-inflation patch later stretched apart. The **flatness problem**: $\Omega$ is suspiciously close to 1 — solved because exponential stretching drives $\Omega \to 1$ exponentially fast. As a bonus, quantum fluctuations are stretched to cosmic scale, seeding **cmb-anisotropies** and **large-scale-structure**.

### Where it connects
Inflation explains the flatness measured in **critical-density**, seeds the **cmb-anisotropies**, and predicts **primordial-gravitational-waves**. Its "never quite ending" variants spawn the **multiverse-inflation-debate**.

### Watch out
Inflation's testable prediction is a *nearly* scale-invariant spectrum with a slight red tilt, $n_s \approx 0.965$ — confirmed by the CMB. The smoking-gun B-mode gravitational-wave signal has *not* been detected (see the BICEP2 episode), so inflation is strongly supported but not proven, and the inflaton's identity remains unknown.

atoms.title: Baryogenesis
atoms.summary: Some unknown process produced slightly more matter than antimatter, leaving the matter we see today.

depths.eli5: Every particle of matter has a mirror-image 'antimatter' twin, and when a particle meets its twin they wipe each other out in a flash of light. In the hot early universe there was nearly as much antimatter as matter, so almost everything annihilated. But for every billion-and-one bits of matter there were only a billion bits of antimatter — a tiny imbalance. After all the pairs cancelled, that leftover one-in-a-billion sliver of matter is everything we see: every star, planet, and person.
depths.core: 'Antimatter' is a counterpart to ordinary matter with opposite electric charge; when a particle meets its antiparticle they 'annihilate,' converting into radiation. A 'baryon' is a heavy particle like a proton or neutron — the building blocks of atomic nuclei. If matter and antimatter had been made in exactly equal amounts, they'd have annihilated completely and left a universe of pure light with no atoms. Instead a tiny surplus of matter — about one extra baryon for every billion photons of light — survived. Producing that surplus requires three ingredients spelled out by physicist Andrei Sakharov: (1) baryon number must not be perfectly conserved (so the count of baryons can change), (2) there must be 'C and CP violation' (a built-in lopsidedness so matter and antimatter aren't treated identically), and (3) the universe must fall out of perfect thermal balance ('equilibrium') at the right moment.
depths.deep: The Standard Model contains all three Sakharov ingredients in principle but provides far too little CP violation and too weak a departure from equilibrium to explain the observed baryon-to-photon ratio η ≈ 6×10⁻¹⁰ — so baryogenesis is strong evidence for physics beyond the Standard Model.

quiz.prompt: Roughly how large was the matter–antimatter asymmetry that survived?
quiz.answer: About one extra baryon per billion photons (baryon-to-photon ratio η ≈ 6×10⁻¹⁰).

quiz.prompt: Why is baryogenesis considered evidence for physics beyond the Standard Model?
quiz.answer: The Standard Model's CP violation and out-of-equilibrium dynamics are far too weak to produce the observed asymmetry, so new physics is required.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Every matter particle has an antimatter twin with opposite charge; when a particle meets its twin, they annihilate into light. In the hot early universe there was *nearly* as much antimatter as matter, so almost everything annihilated. But for every billion-and-one bits of matter there were only a billion bits of antimatter — a tiny imbalance. After the pairs cancelled, that leftover one-in-a-billion sliver of matter became everything: every star, planet, and person.

### Precisely
**Baryogenesis** is whatever process generated the matter–antimatter asymmetry. A **baryon** is a proton or neutron. The asymmetry is captured by the **baryon-to-photon ratio**:
$$\eta = \frac{n_B - n_{\bar B}}{n_\gamma} \approx 6\times10^{-10}$$
i.e. about six extra baryons per ten billion photons.

### Worked example
If matter and antimatter were *exactly* equal, annihilation would leave $n_B/n_\gamma \sim 10^{-18}$ — a universe of nearly pure light with essentially no atoms. The observed $\eta \approx 6\times10^{-10}$ is about a *billion* times larger, so roughly **one baryon per billion survived** the great annihilation; the other billion-minus-one cancelled with antibaryons into the photons we now see as the CMB.

### Why it's true / how it works
Andrei Sakharov showed that generating $\eta$ from a symmetric start requires **three conditions**: (1) **baryon-number violation** (so the baryon count can change); (2) **C and CP violation** (a built-in lopsidedness so matter and antimatter are not treated identically); (3) **departure from thermal equilibrium** (so the imbalance is not immediately undone). All three must occur together.

### Where it connects
Baryogenesis sets the $\eta$ that the **bbn** light-element yields depend on, and fixes the ordinary-matter budget that **lambda-cdm** balances against dark matter. Its timing is governed by **thermal-history**.

### Watch out
The Standard Model contains all three Sakharov ingredients *in principle*, but its CP violation is far too small and its electroweak transition too smooth to produce the observed $\eta$. So baryogenesis is strong evidence for **physics beyond the Standard Model** — the mechanism is genuinely unknown.

atoms.title: Big Bang nucleosynthesis
atoms.summary: In the first few minutes the universe forged the light elements; their measured abundances match the prediction precisely.

depths.eli5: When the universe was just a few minutes old it was hot and dense enough to act like a giant nuclear furnace, cooking the simplest atomic nuclei — mostly hydrogen and helium. Here's the amazing part: when astronomers measure how much hydrogen and helium the universe actually has today, the amounts match what this few-minute furnace should have made. That agreement is one of the strongest reasons to trust the Big Bang picture.
depths.core: 'Nucleosynthesis' means building atomic nuclei. A nucleus is the dense core of an atom, made of protons and neutrons. 'Nuclear fusion' is when small nuclei stick together to form bigger ones, releasing energy. Between about one second and a few minutes after the Big Bang, the universe was hot and dense enough for fusion to run. Protons and neutrons fused into 'deuterium' (a heavy form of hydrogen), then mostly into 'helium-4' (about 25% of all ordinary matter by weight), plus a trace of 'lithium-7' — and essentially nothing heavier (those came much later inside stars). How much of each formed depends sensitively on the 'baryon-to-photon ratio' (how many ordinary matter particles there were per particle of light). The predicted amounts match the measured ones beautifully — a landmark success of cosmology.
depths.deep: Deuterium is the most sensitive 'baryometer': its abundance pins the baryon density independently of the CMB, and the two agree, strongly constraining how much ordinary (baryonic) matter exists — far less than the total matter, which is why most matter must be non-baryonic.

quiz.answer: About 25% of ordinary (baryonic) matter by mass, with the rest mostly hydrogen and traces of deuterium and lithium.

quiz.answer: BBN fixes the baryon density (via deuterium especially) at a value far below the total matter density inferred from gravity, so most matter cannot be baryons.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
When the universe was a few minutes old it was hot and dense enough to act like a giant nuclear furnace, cooking the simplest nuclei — mostly hydrogen and helium. The amazing part: when astronomers measure how much hydrogen and helium the universe actually contains, the amounts match what this few-minute furnace should have made. That agreement is one of the strongest reasons to trust the Big Bang.

### Precisely
**Big Bang nucleosynthesis** (BBN) is the fusion of light nuclei in the window $t \approx 1\,\text{s}$ to a few minutes, when $T$ fell from $\sim10^{10}\,\text{K}$ to $\sim10^{9}\,\text{K}$. Protons and neutrons fused into deuterium ($^2$H), then mostly $^4$He, with traces of $^3$He and $^7$Li. The predicted **helium mass fraction** is $Y_p \approx 0.247$ — about a quarter of ordinary matter by mass — with essentially nothing heavier (heavier elements await stars).

### Worked example
The helium fraction is roughly fixed by the neutron-to-proton ratio at freeze-out. Around $T \approx 0.8\,\text{MeV}$ the ratio froze near $n/p \approx 1/7$. Essentially all neutrons end up in $^4$He (2 neutrons + 2 protons each), so
$$Y_p \approx \frac{2 (n/p)}{1 + (n/p)} = \frac{2/7}{8/7} = 0.25,$$
matching observation — a clean, parameter-light prediction.

### Why it's true / how it works
The yields depend sensitively on the **baryon-to-photon ratio** $\eta$ from **baryogenesis**. More baryons mean faster fusion and slightly more helium but much *less* leftover deuterium. **Deuterium** is so fragile that it serves as the best "baryometer": its measured abundance pins $\eta$, and the value agrees with the entirely independent **acoustic-peaks** determination.

### Where it connects
BBN fixes the baryon density $\Omega_b$ — and crucially, $\Omega_b \ll \Omega_m$, meaning most matter is *non-baryonic* **dark-matter**. It is one of the three pillars of the **big-bang** and a cornerstone of **lambda-cdm**.

### Watch out
BBN only makes the *lightest* elements; carbon, oxygen, iron, and everything heavier were forged later in stars and supernovae. Also, the lithium-7 prediction is somewhat *higher* than observed — the "lithium problem," a real (if minor) open puzzle.

atoms.title: Recombination and last scattering
atoms.summary: At ~380,000 years the universe cooled enough for atoms to form, releasing the light we now see as the CMB.

depths.eli5: Imagine thick fog: light can't travel far because it keeps bouncing off the droplets. The early universe was like that — a glowing fog of electrically charged particles that constantly scattered light, so nothing could shine through. Then it cooled enough for those particles to pair up into ordinary atoms, the fog cleared all at once, and the trapped light suddenly flew free in every direction. That freed light is what we now detect as the cosmic microwave background.
depths.core: Before this moment the universe was a 'plasma' — a hot soup where electrons (tiny negative particles) roamed free instead of being attached to atoms. Free electrons are very good at scattering light ('photons'), bouncing them around endlessly, so the universe was 'opaque' (you couldn't see through it). As it expanded and cooled to about 3000 K — at redshift z ≈ 1100, roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang — electrons finally combined with protons to form neutral hydrogen atoms. This event is called 'recombination.' With the free electrons gone, photons stopped scattering and streamed freely; the universe became 'transparent.' The shell of space from which that last-scattered light reaches us is called the 'surface of last scattering,' and the light from it is the cosmic microwave background.
depths.deep: Recombination is not instantaneous — it has finite thickness in redshift, which slightly smears the smallest CMB features; the relevant transition is set by the balance of recombination and ionization (Saha/Peebles equations), and the residual free-electron fraction matters for CMB damping at small scales.

atoms.note: The CMB photons have been traveling freely for ~13.8 billion years, redshifted from ~3000 K to 2.725 K.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Picture thick fog: light cannot travel far because it scatters off the droplets. The early universe was like that — a glowing fog of charged particles that endlessly scattered light, so nothing shone through. Then it cooled enough for those particles to pair into neutral atoms, the fog cleared all at once, and the trapped light flew free in every direction. That freed light is what we now detect as the **cmb-origin**.

### Precisely
**Recombination** is the epoch when free electrons combined with protons to form neutral hydrogen:
$$p + e^- \rightarrow \text{H} + \gamma.$$
It occurred at redshift $z \approx 1100$, temperature $T \approx 3000\,\text{K}$, about **380,000 years** after the Big Bang. Before it, the universe was an ionized **plasma** (free electrons + nuclei) that was *opaque* — photons scattered off free electrons via Thomson scattering. After it, the universe became *transparent*, and photons streamed freely from the **surface of last scattering**.

### Worked example
Why $\sim3000\,\text{K}$ and not hydrogen's $13.6\,\text{eV}$ ionization energy ($\sim158{,}000\,\text{K}$)? Because there were a *billion* photons per baryon (the inverse of $\eta$), the rare high-energy photons in the tail kept hydrogen ionized until the temperature dropped well below the naive value. Using **thermal-history**, $T = 2.725\times1101 \approx 3000\,\text{K}$ — consistent.

### Why it's true / how it works
Free electrons scatter photons efficiently; remove them and the scattering stops. As expansion cooled the plasma below $\sim3000\,\text{K}$, electrons could finally bind to protons faster than energetic photons could re-ionize them. The free-electron fraction plummeted, the photon mean free path shot up past the horizon, and the photons decoupled.

### Where it connects
Recombination releases the **cmb-origin**; the snapshot it leaves carries the **cmb-anisotropies** and **acoustic-peaks** that encode the cosmological parameters. It is dated using **thermal-history**.

### Watch out
The name is a misnomer — the electrons and protons were *never* combined before, so nothing "re-" combined. Also, recombination is not instantaneous: it has finite thickness in redshift, which slightly blurs the smallest CMB features.

atoms.title: The cosmic microwave background
atoms.summary: A near-perfect 2.725 K blackbody glow filling the sky — the relic radiation from last scattering.

depths.eli5: Point a sensitive radio antenna anywhere in the sky and you'll pick up a faint, even hum of microwaves coming from every direction. That hum is leftover light from when the universe became see-through, almost 14 billion years ago. It is the oldest light in existence — a baby photo of the entire cosmos.
depths.core: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is the light released at recombination, when the universe first became transparent. Since then, expansion has stretched that light enormously, shifting it from a hot glow into the 'microwave' band (the same family of waves as in a microwave oven, but extremely faint) and cooling it to just 2.725 K — only a few degrees above absolute zero. Its 'spectrum' (the brightness at each wavelength) is the most perfect 'blackbody' ever measured in nature — a blackbody being the precise glow that any object in thermal balance gives off — which proves the early universe really was a hot, uniform soup. It was discovered by accident by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson in 1965, and it is the most direct evidence we have of the hot Big Bang.
depths.deep: The CMB is isotropic to about 1 part in 100,000 after removing our motion (the dipole from the Sun's ~370 km/s peculiar velocity); its tiny residual anisotropies encode the initial conditions and contents of the universe, making it cosmology's richest single data set.

atoms.note: COBE (1990s) measured the blackbody spectrum; WMAP and Planck mapped the anisotropies.
