atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Point a sensitive radio antenna anywhere in the sky and you pick up a faint, even hum of microwaves from every direction. That hum is leftover light from when the universe became transparent, nearly 14 billion years ago. It is the oldest light in existence — a baby photo of the entire cosmos.

### Precisely
The **cosmic microwave background** (CMB) is the relic radiation released at **recombination**. Expansion has stretched it by a factor $\sim1100$, cooling it to a present temperature of $T_0 = 2.725\,\text{K}$ and shifting its peak into the microwave band. Its spectrum is the most perfect **blackbody** ever measured in nature, following the Planck law
$$B_\nu(T) = \frac{2h\nu^3}{c^2}\frac{1}{e^{h\nu/k_BT} - 1}$$
with deviations smaller than $\sim50$ parts per million (measured by COBE/FIRAS).

### Worked example
Wien's displacement law gives the peak wavelength: $\lambda_{\text{peak}} = b/T = (2.90\times10^{-3}\,\text{m·K})/(2.725\,\text{K}) \approx 1.06\times10^{-3}\,\text{m} \approx 1.1\,\text{mm}$ — squarely in the microwave band, which is why it is called the *microwave* background. There are roughly $410$ CMB photons per cubic centimeter of space everywhere.

### Why it's true / how it works
A perfect blackbody requires thermal equilibrium in a hot, opaque medium — exactly the pre-recombination plasma. Expansion then preserves the blackbody form while cooling it (see **thermal-history**), so the near-perfect Planck spectrum today is *direct evidence* the early universe was hot and in equilibrium. Penzias and Wilson discovered it by accident in 1965.

### Where it connects
The CMB is the single richest dataset in cosmology: its **cmb-anisotropies** and **acoustic-peaks** measure the geometry, baryon density, and dark matter density that define **lambda-cdm**. It is the second pillar of the **big-bang**.

### Watch out
The CMB is *not* uniform at the finest level: after removing the dipole from our $\sim370\,\text{km/s}$ motion, residual anisotropies of $\sim1$ part in $10^5$ remain — and those tiny ripples, not the smoothness, carry the cosmological information.

atoms.title: CMB anisotropies
atoms.summary: Tiny temperature ripples (~1 part in 100,000) across the CMB are the seeds of all cosmic structure.

depths.eli5: The leftover CMB glow looks smooth, but if you measure it incredibly carefully you find it's not perfectly even — there are extremely faint hot spots and cold spots, like very slight mottling. Those spots are a map of the tiny lumps that existed in the baby universe, and those lumps are exactly the seeds that gravity later grew into galaxies and galaxy clusters.
depths.core: 'Anisotropy' just means 'not the same in every direction' — here, tiny differences in the CMB temperature from one patch of sky to another. After subtracting the smooth shift caused by our own motion through space, the temperature varies by only about one part in 100,000 — astonishingly uniform, yet not perfectly so. These variations trace the 'density fluctuations' present at recombination: regions that were slightly denser were slightly hotter and show up as warm spots. Inflation makes specific predictions about the statistical pattern of these spots — they should be 'nearly scale-invariant' (similar strength across sizes), 'Gaussian' (randomly distributed like familiar bell-curve noise), and 'adiabatic' (all components fluctuating together) — and every one of those predictions has been confirmed by satellite measurements.
depths.deep: The anisotropies are decomposed in spherical harmonics into an angular power spectrum C_ℓ; the pattern of correlations at each angular scale encodes the geometry, baryon density, dark matter density, and expansion rate — fitting the C_ℓ curve is how the precise cosmological parameters are extracted.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
The leftover CMB glow looks smooth, but measure it precisely enough and it is not perfectly even — extremely faint hot spots and cold spots mottle the sky. Those spots map the tiny lumps that existed in the baby universe, and those lumps are exactly the seeds gravity later grew into galaxies and clusters.

### Precisely
**Anisotropy** means "not the same in every direction." After subtracting the dipole from our motion, the CMB temperature varies by $\Delta T/T \approx 10^{-5}$ (about $\pm30\,\mu\text{K}$ on a $2.725\,\text{K}$ background). The pattern is decomposed in **spherical harmonics**,
$$\frac{\Delta T}{T}(\theta,\phi) = \sum_{\ell m} a_{\ell m} Y_{\ell m}(\theta,\phi),$$
and summarized by the **angular power spectrum** $C_\ell = \langle |a_{\ell m}|^2\rangle$, where multipole $\ell$ corresponds to angular scale $\sim 180^\circ/\ell$.

### Worked example
The famous "first peak" sits near $\ell \approx 220$, corresponding to an angular scale of $\sim 180^\circ/220 \approx 0.8^\circ$ on the sky — about 1.6 times the angular size of the full Moon. That this scale matches the predicted **acoustic-peaks** sound horizon for a *flat* universe is how the CMB confirms $\Omega_{\text{tot}} \approx 1$.

### Why it's true / how it works
The hot and cold spots trace **density fluctuations** at **recombination**: slightly denser regions were slightly hotter (and gravitationally redshifted), appearing as warm spots. **Inflation** predicts these fluctuations are nearly *scale-invariant* ($n_s \approx 0.965$), *Gaussian* (bell-curve random), and *adiabatic* (all components fluctuate together) — and WMAP and Planck confirmed all three.

### Where it connects
The $C_\ell$ spectrum, especially the **acoustic-peaks**, fixes the parameters of **lambda-cdm**. These fluctuations are the seeds of **gravitational-instability** and **large-scale-structure**, and the polarization carries **primordial-gravitational-waves** information.

### Watch out
Do not confuse the $\sim10^{-5}$ anisotropies with the much larger ($\sim10^{-3}$) **dipole**, which is just our own motion through the CMB rest frame and must be subtracted first. The cosmological signal lives in the tiny residual.

atoms.title: Acoustic peaks and the sound horizon
atoms.summary: Sound waves in the early plasma froze in at recombination, leaving a series of peaks that act as a cosmic ruler.

depths.eli5: Before atoms formed, the universe was a hot soup that could carry sound waves, and it literally rang like a struck bell — but a bell whose tone is frozen in place the instant the universe became transparent. That frozen ringing left a pattern of preferred 'loud' and 'quiet' sizes in the CMB spots. Because we know exactly how far sound could travel before the ringing stopped, that pattern works as a ruler we can hold up to the sky to measure the universe's shape and ingredients.
depths.core: A 'sound wave' is just a pressure ripple traveling through a medium. Before recombination, the push of light ('photon pressure') and the pull of gravity together drove sound waves through the 'baryon–photon plasma' (the soup of ordinary matter and light). The farthest such a wave could travel before recombination froze everything is called the 'sound horizon' — a fixed, known length. When you chart the CMB spots by their angular size (the 'angular power spectrum,' a graph of how much variation appears at each spot-size on the sky), this frozen scale shows up as a series of bumps called 'acoustic peaks.' The angular position of the first peak acts as a 'standard ruler': comparing its known true size to its apparent size on the sky reveals whether space is flat. The relative heights of the peaks weigh how much ordinary matter and dark matter the universe holds.
depths.deep: The first peak sits at ℓ ≈ 220, and its location pins Ω_total ≈ 1 (flat geometry); the ratio of odd to even peak heights reflects baryon loading, and the third-peak height constrains the dark matter density — this is how the CMB delivers percent-level cosmological parameters.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Before atoms formed, the universe was a hot soup that could carry sound waves — and it literally rang like a struck bell, a bell whose tone froze in place the instant the universe became transparent. That frozen ringing left a pattern of preferred "loud" and "quiet" spot-sizes in the CMB. Because we know exactly how far sound could travel before the ringing stopped, that pattern is a ruler we hold up to the sky.

### Precisely
In the pre-recombination **baryon–photon plasma**, photon pressure pushed outward while gravity pulled inward, driving **acoustic oscillations**. The **sound horizon** $r_s = \int_0^{t_{\text{rec}}} c_s\,dt/a$ — the comoving distance a sound wave traveled by recombination — is $\sim150\,\text{Mpc}$ comoving. The sound speed is $c_s = c/\sqrt{3(1+R)}$, where $R \propto \Omega_b$. These oscillations imprint a series of **acoustic peaks** in the CMB **angular power spectrum** $C_\ell$.

### Worked example
The first peak at $\ell_1 \approx 220$ acts as a **standard ruler**: comparing the known physical size $r_s$ to its observed angular size $\theta_1 \approx 0.8^\circ$ tests geometry. In a *closed* universe the spot would look larger (peak at lower $\ell$); in *open*, smaller (higher $\ell$). The observed $\ell_1 \approx 220$ corresponds to $\Omega_{\text{tot}} \approx 1.00$ — spatial flatness.

### Why it's true / how it works
Modes that reached maximum compression or rarefaction exactly at recombination appear loudest, producing harmonic peaks at $\ell \approx 220, 540, 800, \dots$. The *odd* peaks (compressions) are enhanced relative to *even* peaks (rarefactions) by **baryon loading**: more baryons add inertia, deepening compressions. So the odd/even height ratio measures $\Omega_b$, and the third-peak height constrains the **dark-matter** density.

### Where it connects
Acoustic peaks deliver percent-level **lambda-cdm** parameters: $\Omega_b$, $\Omega_c$, $\Omega_k$, and $H_0$. The *same* physics in matter is the **baryon-acoustic-oscillations** standard ruler, and the geometry test refines **critical-density**.

### Watch out
The "sound" is real pressure waves in plasma, *not* sound traveling through vacuum today. And the peaks are in *angular* (statistical) space, not literal hot rings on the sky — they emerge only after computing the power spectrum over the whole map.

atoms.title: Gravitational instability
atoms.summary: Slightly denser regions pull in more matter and grow denser still — gravity amplifies tiny seeds into structure.

depths.eli5: Gravity rewards greed. A patch of space with a little extra matter pulls in nearby matter, which makes it heavier, which makes it pull harder, which makes it heavier still — a runaway snowball effect. Start with the faint lumps recorded in the CMB and let this run for billions of years, and those lumps grow into galaxies and clusters of galaxies.
depths.core: 'Gravitational instability' is the runaway by which small lumps grow into big ones. The tiny density differences imprinted in the CMB ('density fluctuations') are slightly overdense regions; their extra gravity attracts surrounding matter, which raises their 'density contrast' (how much denser they are than average), which strengthens their gravity further. In a static universe this would blow up explosively, but our universe is expanding, and that expansion (the Hubble expansion) constantly pulls matter apart, fighting the collapse. The tug-of-war means the lumps grow only gradually — as a power of the scale factor rather than exponentially — yet over billions of years they amplify enough to assemble all the galaxies and clusters we see.
depths.deep: In the matter-dominated era the density contrast δ grows linearly with the scale factor (δ ∝ a) while perturbations are small; once δ approaches 1 the growth turns nonlinear and regions collapse and virialize — the regime that simulations, not linear theory, must handle.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Gravity rewards greed. A patch with a little extra matter pulls in nearby matter, which makes it heavier, which makes it pull harder, which makes it heavier still — a runaway snowball. Start from the faint lumps recorded in the CMB and let this run for billions of years, and those lumps grow into galaxies and clusters.

### Precisely
**Gravitational instability** is the amplification of small **density fluctuations**. Define the **density contrast** $\delta(\mathbf{x}) = (\rho - \bar\rho)/\bar\rho$. In the linear regime ($|\delta| \ll 1$) during matter domination, it obeys
$$\ddot\delta + 2H\dot\delta = 4\pi G \bar\rho\,\delta,$$
where the $2H\dot\delta$ term is **Hubble friction** from cosmic expansion fighting the collapse. The growing solution is $\delta \propto a$ — linear in the **scale-factor**, not exponential.

### Worked example
The CMB shows $\delta \approx 10^{-5}$ at **recombination** ($a \approx 1/1100$). Growing as $\delta \propto a$ until matter–$\Lambda$ equality, $\delta$ amplifies by a factor $\sim1100$ to $\delta \sim 10^{-2}$ — still small. Nonlinear collapse ($\delta \sim 1$) then proceeds rapidly in the densest regions, which is why galaxies exist today despite tiny initial seeds.

### Why it's true / how it works
In a *static* universe, overdensities would grow *exponentially* — Jeans instability. But our universe *expands*, constantly diluting matter and draining the collapse via the Hubble-friction term. The tug-of-war slows growth to a mere power law ($\delta \propto a$), which is exactly why it took billions of years to build structure.

### Where it connects
It converts **cmb-anisotropies** seeds into **dark-matter-halos** and **large-scale-structure**. Because **dark-matter** ignores radiation pressure, it begins collapsing before baryons, giving structure a head start.

### Watch out
Linear theory ($\delta \propto a$) only holds while $\delta \ll 1$. Once $\delta \sim 1$, the growth turns nonlinear, regions collapse and **virialize**, and only N-body simulations — not the linear equation — can follow what happens.

atoms.title: Evidence for dark matter
atoms.summary: Galaxies rotate too fast, clusters bind too tightly, and lensing is too strong for the visible matter alone.

depths.eli5: Watch the stars at the outer edge of a spinning galaxy. They whirl around so fast that the gravity of everything we can see — all the stars and gas — should not be enough to hold them in; they ought to fly off. They don't. So something we can't see must be there, adding extra gravity. We call that unseen stuff 'dark matter,' and several totally different observations all point to it.
depths.core: 'Dark matter' is matter that gives off no light but still has gravity. Several independent clues all demand far more gravitating mass than the visible stars and gas can supply: (1) 'galaxy rotation curves' — plots of how fast stars orbit versus their distance from the center — stay flat far out, instead of dropping off as visible matter predicts; (2) galaxies inside clusters zip around too fast to stay bound by visible mass alone; (3) 'gravitational lensing' (the bending of light by mass) is stronger than the visible matter can account for; and (4) the heights of the CMB acoustic peaks require it. All four converge on an unseen, 'non-baryonic' component (not made of ordinary protons and neutrons) about five times more abundant than ordinary matter.
depths.deep: The Bullet Cluster is a striking case: in a cluster collision the hot gas (most of the baryons) lags behind while the lensing mass tracks the galaxies, spatially separating the bulk of the mass from the bulk of the baryons — hard to explain by modifying gravity alone.

quiz.answer: Flat galaxy rotation curves and gravitational lensing / cluster dynamics that exceed what visible matter can explain (also the CMB peak heights).

quiz.answer: The lensing mass is spatially offset from the dominant baryonic component (the hot gas), so the gravitating mass is not where most of the ordinary matter is.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Watch the stars at a spinning galaxy's outer edge. They whirl so fast that the gravity of everything visible — all the stars and gas — should not hold them in; they ought to fly off. They do not. So something unseen must be there, adding gravity. We call it **dark matter**, and several completely independent observations all point to it.

### Precisely
**Dark matter** is matter that emits no light but exerts gravity. Multiple independent probes demand far more gravitating mass than visible matter supplies:
1. **Galaxy rotation curves** stay *flat* at large radius, $v(r) \approx \text{const}$, instead of falling as $v \propto r^{-1/2}$.
2. **Cluster velocity dispersions** (Zwicky, 1933) imply masses far exceeding visible matter.
3. **Gravitational lensing** is stronger than luminous mass can produce.
4. **CMB acoustic-peaks** heights require a non-baryonic component.
All converge on $\Omega_{\text{dm}} \approx 0.27$, about five times $\Omega_b \approx 0.05$.

### Worked example
For a flat rotation curve, $v \approx \text{const}$ requires enclosed mass $M(r) = v^2 r/G \propto r$ — mass keeps growing linearly with radius even where no stars are visible. For the Milky Way, $v \approx 220\,\text{km/s}$ out to $r \approx 50\,\text{kpc}$ gives $M \sim v^2 r/G \approx 5\times10^{11}\,M_\odot$ — several times the visible stellar mass.

### Why it's true / how it works
The **Bullet Cluster** is the decisive case: in a cluster collision, the hot X-ray gas (most of the *baryons*) lags behind, while gravitational **lensing** shows the bulk of the mass tracking the nearly collisionless galaxies. The mass and the baryons are *spatially separated* — exactly what collisionless dark matter predicts and hard to fake by modifying gravity.

### Where it connects
Dark matter seeds **dark-matter-halos**, enables **gravitational-instability** to build **large-scale-structure**, and is the "CDM" in **lambda-cdm**. **bbn** independently shows most matter is non-baryonic.

### Watch out
Dark matter is not "missing" or hypothetical hand-waving — it is *inferred* from gravity by many independent methods that agree. Modified-gravity alternatives (MOND) fit rotation curves but struggle with the Bullet Cluster and CMB peaks simultaneously.

atoms.title: Dark matter halos
atoms.summary: Dark matter collapses first into extended halos; galaxies form as gas falls into these gravitational wells.

depths.eli5: Invisible dark matter clumps together into big roughly-round blobs first. Later, ordinary gas drains down into the middle of each blob — like water collecting in a bowl — and that gas lights up into the stars and galaxies we can actually see. So every glowing galaxy sits at the heart of a much bigger, invisible blob.
depths.core: A 'halo' here is a large, roughly spherical cloud of dark matter surrounding a galaxy. Dark matter clumps before ordinary matter does, and the reason is subtle: before recombination, ordinary matter ('baryons') was held smooth by the constant push of light ('radiation pressure'), but dark matter ignores light entirely, so it was free to start collapsing earlier. These early dark-matter clumps form 'potential wells' — gravitational valleys. Ordinary gas then falls into those valleys, cools off by radiating away energy as light, and condenses into stars and galaxies at the bottom. The visible galaxy is therefore just the bright tip embedded in a far larger, more massive dark matter halo that supplies most of the gravity.
depths.deep: N-body simulations of cold dark matter produce halos with a near-universal density profile (the NFW form) and a hierarchical merger history — small halos form first and merge into larger ones, a prediction that broadly matches observed galaxy clustering.

quiz.prompt: Why does dark matter begin collapsing into halos before ordinary matter?
quiz.answer: It does not feel radiation pressure, so it can start clumping while baryons are still held smooth by photons before recombination.

quiz.prompt: Explain how galaxies relate to dark matter halos.
quiz.answer: Galaxies form when gas falls into pre-existing dark matter halos, cools, and condenses into stars; the visible galaxy sits at the center of a much larger, more massive dark halo.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Invisible dark matter clumps into big roughly-round blobs first. Later, ordinary gas drains into the middle of each blob — like water collecting in a bowl — and lights up into the stars and galaxies we actually see. So every glowing galaxy sits at the heart of a much bigger, invisible blob.

### Precisely
A **dark matter halo** is a large, roughly spherical, gravitationally bound concentration of dark matter surrounding a galaxy. N-body simulations of **cold dark matter** find a near-universal density profile, the **Navarro–Frenk–White (NFW)** form:
$$\rho(r) = \frac{\rho_0}{(r/r_s)(1 + r/r_s)^2},$$
with scale radius $r_s$. The halo mass typically exceeds the visible galaxy's stellar mass by a factor of $\sim10$–$100$.

### Worked example
For the Milky Way, the visible stellar disk is $\sim6\times10^{10}\,M_\odot$, but its dark halo is estimated at $\sim1\times10^{12}\,M_\odot$ — over ten times more mass, extending several times beyond the visible disk. The flat **rotation curve** (constant $v$) is the direct signature of this extended halo providing $M(r) \propto r$.

### Why it's true / how it works
Dark matter clumps *before* baryons because it does not feel **radiation pressure**. Before **recombination**, photons held the baryons smooth, but dark matter — invisible to light — was free to start collapsing earlier under **gravitational-instability**. Its early potential wells are the "bowls" into which gas later falls, cools by radiating, and condenses into stars.

### Where it connects
Halos are where galaxies form, linking **gravitational-instability** to **large-scale-structure**. Their hierarchical merging (small halos merging into big ones) builds the cosmic web. Halo masses are weighed by **gravitational-lensing**.

### Watch out
The NFW profile predicts a steep central "cusp," but some observed dwarf galaxies show flatter "cores" — the **cusp–core problem**, a genuine small-scale tension in the cold-dark-matter picture. Also, the visible galaxy is just the bright tip; most of a galaxy's mass and extent is dark.

atoms.title: Large-scale structure
atoms.summary: Galaxies trace a cosmic web of filaments, walls, and voids — the largest patterns gravity has built.

depths.eli5: If you map out where all the galaxies are, they don't fill space evenly like sprinkles in batter. Instead they string themselves into glowing threads that wrap around gigantic nearly-empty bubbles — a pattern that looks strikingly like a spiderweb or a sponge. This 'cosmic web' is the biggest structure gravity has ever built.
depths.core: 'Large-scale structure' is the overall arrangement of galaxies across the universe. By measuring millions of galaxy positions ('redshift surveys' — see the redshift-survey atom), astronomers find galaxies organized into a 'cosmic web': long 'filaments' (threads) and 'sheets' (walls) of galaxies surrounding huge nearly-empty regions called 'voids,' with dense clusters of galaxies sitting where the filaments cross. This web is the grown-up result of gravitational instability acting on the faint seeds seen in the CMB. Statisticians describe it with tools like the 'two-point correlation function' (how much more likely two galaxies are to sit a given distance apart than by chance) and the 'power spectrum' (how clustering strength varies with size); both encode the matter density and the nature of dark matter.
depths.deep: Cold dark matter predicts this web in detail; the observed clustering (including the baryon acoustic oscillation feature at ~150 Mpc) matches simulations, while a hot (fast-moving) dark matter would have erased small-scale structure — a key reason dark matter is believed to be 'cold'.

quiz.answer: A cosmic web of filaments and sheets around large voids, with clusters at the intersections.

quiz.prompt: Why does the existence of fine-grained cosmic-web structure argue for COLD rather than hot dark matter?
quiz.answer: Fast-moving (hot) dark matter would free-stream out of small overdensities and wash out small-scale structure; the observed sharp structure requires slow-moving (cold) dark matter.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Map where all the galaxies are and they do not fill space evenly like sprinkles in batter. Instead they string into glowing threads wrapping gigantic nearly-empty bubbles — a pattern resembling a spiderweb or a sponge. This **cosmic web** is the largest structure gravity has ever built.

### Precisely
**Large-scale structure** is the arrangement of matter on scales of millions to hundreds of millions of light-years: **filaments** (threads) and **walls** (sheets) of galaxies surrounding huge **voids**, with dense **clusters** at the nodes where filaments cross. It is quantified statistically by the **two-point correlation function** $\xi(r)$ — the excess probability over random of finding two galaxies separated by $r$ — and its Fourier transform, the **power spectrum** $P(k)$.

### Worked example
The galaxy correlation function is well fit on intermediate scales by a power law, $\xi(r) \approx (r/r_0)^{-1.8}$ with $r_0 \approx 5\,\text{Mpc}/h$. So galaxies $1\,\text{Mpc}$ apart are $\sim5^{1.8} \approx 17$ times more likely to be neighbors than random — strong clustering. Superimposed is a faint bump at $\sim150\,\text{Mpc}$: the **baryon-acoustic-oscillations** feature.

### Why it's true / how it works
The cosmic web is **gravitational-instability** acting on the **cmb-anisotropies** seeds inside **dark-matter-halos**. Matter flows out of voids, along filaments, into clusters — a flow simulations reproduce in detail. The observed sharp, fine-grained structure requires **cold** (slow-moving) dark matter; **hot** dark matter would free-stream out of small overdensities and erase them.

### Where it connects
It is mapped by **redshift-surveys**, encodes the **baryon-acoustic-oscillations** ruler, and its statistics constrain the matter density and dark-energy behavior in **lambda-cdm** and **dark-energy-equation-of-state**.

### Watch out
The cosmic web's apparent "structures" (like the Sloan Great Wall) are still consistent with the **cosmological-principle**, which holds only on yet-larger averaging scales. Below $\sim100\,\text{Mpc}$ the universe is genuinely lumpy; above it, smooth.

atoms.title: Baryon acoustic oscillations
atoms.summary: The same early sound waves left a ~150 Mpc preferred separation between galaxies — a standard ruler in 3D.

depths.eli5: Remember the early universe rang like a bell (the acoustic-peaks atom)? That same ringing left a subtle fingerprint in where galaxies ended up: pairs of galaxies are very slightly more likely to sit about 500 million light-years apart than any other distance. Because that special separation is a fixed, known length, astronomers use it as a giant tape measure to gauge distances and track how the universe has expanded.
depths.core: The same sound waves that left the acoustic peaks in the CMB also stamped a faint preferred distance into the arrangement of matter: galaxies are slightly more likely to be separated by the 'sound horizon,' about 150 megaparsecs ('comoving,' meaning measured in today's stretched-out units; that's roughly 500 million light-years). This shows up as a small bump in the 'galaxy correlation function' (the graph of how galaxy-pair counts depend on separation). Because the true length of this 'baryon acoustic oscillation' (BAO) feature is known, it serves as a 'standard ruler': by measuring how big it appears at different redshifts (different cosmic eras), astronomers chart the expansion history of the universe.
depths.deep: Because the BAO scale is set by early-universe physics measurable from the CMB, it is a 'calibrated' ruler; comparing its apparent size across redshift constrains H(z) and the dark energy equation of state largely independently of the supernova distance ladder.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Remember the early universe rang like a bell (the **acoustic-peaks**)? That same ringing left a fingerprint in where galaxies ended up: pairs of galaxies are very slightly more likely to sit about 500 million light-years apart than any other distance. Because that special separation is a fixed, known length, astronomers use it as a giant tape measure to track cosmic expansion.

### Precisely
**Baryon acoustic oscillations** (BAO) are the imprint of the pre-recombination sound waves on the *matter* distribution. The **sound horizon** $r_s \approx 150\,\text{Mpc}$ comoving ($\approx 500$ million light-years) appears as a single bump in the galaxy **two-point correlation function** $\xi(r)$ at $r = r_s$, equivalently as wiggles in the **power spectrum** $P(k)$. Because $r_s$ is calibrated by early-universe physics, BAO is a **standard ruler**.

### Worked example
Measure the BAO bump's *apparent* angular size $\theta(z)$ and redshift extent $\Delta z$ in a galaxy survey at redshift $z$. The angular size gives the angular-diameter distance $D_A(z) = r_s/[(1+z)\theta]$; the radial extent gives the expansion rate $H(z) = c\,\Delta z/r_s$. Doing this at several redshifts maps $H(z)$ directly — independent of the **standard-candles** ladder.

### Why it's true / how it works
At **recombination**, the outward-traveling pressure wave around each overdensity froze, leaving a faint shell of enhanced density at radius $r_s$ around every initial peak. Billions of years later, galaxies preferentially form both at the original center *and* on that shell, producing the excess-probability bump at $r_s$ — the same physics as the CMB **acoustic-peaks**, now in 3D matter.

### Where it connects
BAO is one of the most powerful **dark-energy** probes, constraining $H(z)$ and the **dark-energy-equation-of-state** $w$. It is measured in **redshift-surveys** (SDSS/BOSS/DESI) and cross-calibrated against the CMB.

### Watch out
The BAO bump is *small* — a few-percent excess on top of the smooth correlation function — and requires hundreds of thousands of galaxy redshifts to detect statistically. It is a *standard ruler* (fixed length), distinct from a *standard candle* (fixed brightness).

atoms.title: Standard candles
atoms.summary: Objects of known intrinsic brightness let you read distance from how dim they appear.

depths.eli5: If two identical light bulbs are in front of you and one looks dimmer, you instantly know it's farther away. Astronomers use the same trick: if they know how bright an object truly is, they can judge its distance from how bright it merely appears. Certain stars and certain stellar explosions are dependable cosmic 'light bulbs' of known true brightness.
depths.core: A 'standard candle' is any object whose real, intrinsic brightness ('luminosity') is known in advance. Compare that to how bright it looks from Earth and the distance falls out of the 'inverse-square law' — the rule that brightness fades as 1 divided by distance squared (twice as far looks four times dimmer). Two workhorses fill different distance ranges: 'Cepheid variable stars' pulse in size and brightness, and the speed of their pulsing reliably reveals their luminosity, which calibrates distances to nearby galaxies; and 'Type Ia supernovae' — runaway thermonuclear explosions of white-dwarf stars that all peak at nearly the same brightness — are bright enough to be seen billions of light-years away, extending the measurement of the universe's expansion to enormous distances.
depths.deep: The distance ladder is built in rungs (parallax → Cepheids → Type Ia SNe), and each rung's calibration error propagates; Type Ia luminosity is standardized using the light-curve shape (brighter supernovae decline more slowly), without which they would not be precise enough for cosmology.

atoms.note: Type Ia supernovae as standard candles drove the 1998 discovery of accelerating expansion.

quiz.prompt: What property of a standard candle lets it measure distance?
quiz.answer: Its known intrinsic luminosity — comparing it to the observed brightness gives distance via the inverse-square law.

quiz.prompt: Why are Type Ia supernovae especially valuable as standard candles?
quiz.answer: They have nearly uniform (and light-curve-standardizable) peak brightness and are extremely luminous, so they can be seen across cosmological distances to trace the expansion history.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
If two identical bulbs sit before you and one looks dimmer, you instantly know it is farther away. Astronomers use the same trick: knowing an object's true brightness lets them judge its distance from how bright it merely appears. Certain stars and stellar explosions are dependable cosmic "bulbs" of known true brightness.

### Precisely
A **standard candle** is an object of known intrinsic **luminosity** $L$ (power emitted). Its observed **flux** $F$ (power received per area) gives distance via the **inverse-square law**:
$$F = \frac{L}{4\pi d_L^2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad d_L = \sqrt{\frac{L}{4\pi F}},$$
where $d_L$ is the **luminosity distance**. Two workhorses: **Cepheid variables** (pulsating stars whose period reveals $L$) for nearby galaxies, and **Type Ia supernovae** for the far universe.

### Worked example
A Type Ia supernova has peak absolute magnitude $M \approx -19.3$. Observe one at apparent magnitude $m = 20$. The distance modulus is $m - M = 20 - (-19.3) = 39.3$, and $d_L = 10^{(m-M+5)/5}\,\text{pc} = 10^{(39.3+5)/5} = 10^{8.86}\,\text{pc} \approx 7.2\times10^{8}\,\text{pc} \approx 720\,\text{Mpc}$ — over 2 billion light-years.

### Why it's true / how it works
**Type Ia supernovae** are runaway thermonuclear explosions of white dwarfs reaching the Chandrasekhar mass ($\approx1.4\,M_\odot$), so they detonate at a nearly *uniform* mass and hence near-uniform peak brightness. The small spread is corrected using the **Phillips relation**: intrinsically brighter ones decline more slowly, so the light-curve shape standardizes the luminosity to $\sim$few-percent precision.

### Where it connects
Standard candles are the upper rungs of the **cosmic-distance-ladder**, calibrated by **Cepheids** (themselves calibrated by parallax). Type Ia supernovae revealed **dark-energy** in 1998 and anchor the local **hubble-tension** value.

### Watch out
Each method has a limited distance range and inherits calibration from the rung below, so systematic errors (dust extinction, metallicity, supernova standardization) propagate up the ladder — which is precisely where a local-vs-early $H_0$ discrepancy could hide.

atoms.title: Redshift surveys and cosmic mapping
atoms.summary: Measuring millions of galaxy redshifts converts the sky into a 3D map of the universe.

depths.eli5: We already know a galaxy's redshift tells us roughly how far away it is. Now do that for millions of galaxies across the sky, and you can place each one at its proper depth — turning a flat picture of dots into a real three-dimensional map of the universe, showing where the threads and empty bubbles of the cosmic web actually are.
depths.core: A 'redshift survey' is a project that records the 'spectrum' (the rainbow breakdown of light) of huge numbers of galaxies. Each spectrum reveals that galaxy's redshift, which converts to a distance, so the survey can plot every galaxy in three dimensions. Surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) have mapped millions of galaxies this way. The resulting 3D maps reveal the cosmic web directly and let cosmologists extract statistical measurements — the 'galaxy power spectrum' (how strongly galaxies clump at each size scale), the correlation function, and the BAO standard-ruler scale — that pin down what the universe is made of and what shape it has.
depths.deep: Redshift maps are distorted by galaxies' peculiar velocities ('redshift-space distortions'): infall toward overdensities squashes structures along the line of sight, an effect that, rather than being mere noise, measures the growth rate of structure and tests gravity on cosmic scales.

atoms.art_prompt: a wedge diagram of a galaxy redshift survey fanning out from Earth, each galaxy placed by its redshift, revealing filaments and voids

quiz.prompt: What quantity does a redshift survey use to estimate each galaxy's distance?
quiz.answer: The galaxy's redshift, converted to distance via the Hubble law / FRW relation.

quiz.prompt: What are redshift-space distortions and why are they useful rather than just a nuisance?
quiz.answer: Peculiar velocities shift apparent positions along the line of sight; this distortion measures the growth rate of structure and tests gravity on large scales.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
We already know a galaxy's **cosmological-redshift** tells us roughly how far away it is. Do that for *millions* of galaxies across the sky and you can place each one at its proper depth — turning a flat picture of dots into a real three-dimensional map showing where the threads and empty bubbles of the cosmic web actually lie.

### Precisely
A **redshift survey** records the **spectrum** of large numbers of galaxies; each spectrum's redshift $z$ converts to a distance, placing the galaxy in 3D. Two angular coordinates (RA, Dec) plus the redshift-derived distance give full positions. The resulting catalog yields the **power spectrum** $P(k)$, **correlation function** $\xi(r)$, and the **baryon-acoustic-oscillations** ruler. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) has mapped *millions* of galaxies this way; DESI is now mapping tens of millions.

### Worked example
A galaxy at $z = 0.1$ sits at comoving distance $d \approx cz/H_0 = (3\times10^5\,\text{km/s})(0.1)/(70\,\text{km/s/Mpc}) \approx 430\,\text{Mpc}$ (low-$z$ approximation). Repeat for every galaxy in the catalog, bin by separation, and the **baryon-acoustic-oscillations** bump emerges at $\sim150\,\text{Mpc}$ — a literal ruler read off the 3D map.

### Why it's true / how it works
Spectroscopy spreads a galaxy's light into a rainbow; known emission/absorption lines appear shifted by $(1+z)$, giving a precise redshift. Photometric surveys estimate $z$ more crudely from broadband colors for far more objects. Together they reconstruct the **large-scale-structure** in three dimensions.

### Where it connects
Surveys turn **cosmological-redshift** into cosmic cartography, revealing **large-scale-structure**, measuring **baryon-acoustic-oscillations**, and constraining the **dark-energy-equation-of-state**.

### Watch out
Redshift maps suffer **redshift-space distortions**: galaxies' peculiar velocities (infall toward overdensities) add to the cosmological redshift, squashing structures along the line of sight ("Fingers of God" and the Kaiser effect). Far from being mere noise, this distortion *measures* the growth rate of structure and tests gravity — but it must be modeled, not ignored.

atoms.title: Dark energy and accelerating expansion
atoms.summary: Distant supernovae revealed that cosmic expansion is speeding up, driven by a repulsive 'dark energy'.

depths.eli5: You'd expect gravity to be slowly putting the brakes on the universe's expansion — everything pulling on everything else. The shock of 1998 was the opposite: the expansion is actually speeding up. Something invisible is acting like an anti-gravity, pushing space apart, and we call it 'dark energy.'
depths.core: In 1998 two rival teams measured distant Type Ia supernovae (the standard-candle explosions) and found them dimmer — and therefore farther away — than a slowing-down universe should allow. That meant the expansion is 'accelerating' (speeding up). In the Friedmann equations, speeding up requires an ingredient with strongly 'negative pressure' (pressure that pulls inward, here about p ≈ −ρc², where ρ is its energy density and c is the speed of light) — which, counterintuitively, drives space apart on the largest scales. This 'dark energy' makes up roughly 70% of the total energy of the universe and dominates the cosmos today, even though no one yet knows what it actually is.
depths.deep: Acceleration follows from the second Friedmann equation, ä/a ∝ −(ρ + 3p/c²): any component with p < −ρc²/3 pushes ä > 0. Whether dark energy is a constant Λ or evolves (an equation-of-state parameter w possibly ≠ −1) is a central observational question.

atoms.note: The 1998 discovery won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics (Perlmutter, Schmidt, Riess).
sources: arXiv astro-ph (Type Ia SNe, dark energy)

resources.label: Wikipedia — Accelerating expansion of the universe
Wikipedia — Negative pressure (Equation of state, cosmology)

atoms.art_prompt: a Hubble diagram where distant supernovae fall below the decelerating-universe curve, with an expansion timeline bending upward into acceleration

quiz.prompt: What observation first revealed the accelerating expansion of the universe?
quiz.answer: Distant Type Ia supernovae appeared dimmer (farther away) than a decelerating universe would predict, indicating acceleration.

quiz.prompt: From the acceleration equation ä/a ∝ −(ρ + 3p/c²), what condition on pressure produces acceleration?
quiz.answer: A component with p < −ρc²/3 makes the right side positive, so ä > 0 — strongly negative pressure drives accelerated expansion.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
You would expect gravity to slowly brake cosmic expansion — everything pulling on everything else. The shock of 1998 was the opposite: expansion is *speeding up*. Something invisible acts like anti-gravity, pushing space apart. We call it **dark energy**.

### Precisely
**Dark energy** is a component with strongly **negative pressure** that drives accelerated expansion. From the **friedmann-equations** acceleration equation,
$$\frac{\ddot a}{a} = -\frac{4\pi G}{3}\left(\rho + \frac{3p}{c^2}\right),$$
$\ddot a > 0$ requires $p < -\tfrac{1}{3}\rho c^2$. The simplest dark energy has $p = -\rho c^2$ (equation of state $w = -1$). It makes up $\Omega_\Lambda \approx 0.69$ of the cosmic budget and dominates today.

### Worked example
In 1998 the Supernova Cosmology Project and High-z Supernova Search Team found distant Type Ia supernovae at $z \sim 0.5$ about $0.25$ magnitudes *fainter* (hence $\sim10$–$15\%$ farther) than a decelerating, matter-only universe predicts. Fitting the **friedmann-equations** to the supernova **standard-candles** Hubble diagram required $\Omega_\Lambda \approx 0.7$ — acceleration.

### Why it's true / how it works
Why does negative pressure push *outward*? In GR, the source of gravity is $\rho + 3p/c^2$ (pressure gravitates, see **stress-energy**). A sufficiently negative $p$ flips that combination negative, so the gravitational effect becomes *repulsive* on cosmic scales — counterintuitive but a direct consequence of the field equations.

### Where it connects
Dark energy is the "Λ" in **lambda-cdm** and the **cosmological-constant** if $w=-1$. Whether $w$ truly equals $-1$ or evolves is the **dark-energy-equation-of-state** question, and it determines the **cosmic-fate**.

### Watch out
Dark energy is *not* dark matter — dark matter clumps and *attracts*; dark energy is smooth and *repels*. And acceleration does not mean the expansion *rate* $H$ increases — $H$ actually decreases toward a constant; it is $\ddot a$, the growth of $a$ itself, that turns positive.

atoms.title: Cosmological constant Λ
atoms.summary: The simplest dark energy is a constant vacuum energy density — Einstein's Λ, restored to explain acceleration.

depths.eli5: Here's the simplest possible explanation for dark energy: empty space itself carries a fixed amount of energy that never thins out, no matter how much the universe grows. Ordinary matter spreads thinner as space expands, but this energy-of-empty-space stays the same density forever — so as everything else fades, its steady outward push eventually wins and the expansion speeds up.
depths.core: The 'cosmological constant,' written Λ (the Greek letter lambda), is the extra term Einstein once added to his field equations. Treated as dark energy, it behaves like a uniform energy density built into empty space (the 'vacuum') that stays exactly constant over time and has negative pressure. Its 'equation of state' — the ratio of pressure to energy density, labeled w — equals −1, the hallmark of a true constant. Because matter and radiation dilute as the universe expands while Λ does not, Λ inevitably overtakes them and comes to dominate, producing accelerating expansion. It is the simplest dark-energy model and fits current data well, which is why it's the 'Λ' in the standard ΛCDM model.
depths.deep: Identifying Λ with quantum vacuum energy yields a prediction off by ~120 orders of magnitude from the observed value — the 'cosmological constant problem,' one of the deepest unsolved puzzles in physics, plus the 'coincidence problem' of why Λ and matter densities are comparable right now.

atoms.art_prompt: empty space depicted as faintly glowing with constant vacuum energy, its density unchanged across three expansion stages while matter dots thin out

quiz.prompt: What is the equation-of-state parameter w for a cosmological constant?
quiz.answer: w = −1: pressure equals minus the energy density, p = −ρc².

quiz.prompt: Why does the cosmological constant inevitably come to dominate the universe over time?
quiz.answer: Its energy density stays constant while matter and radiation densities dilute as the universe expands, so eventually Λ outweighs everything else.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Here is the simplest possible dark energy: empty space itself carries a fixed energy that never thins out, no matter how much the universe grows. Ordinary matter spreads thinner as space expands, but this energy-of-empty-space stays the same density forever — so as everything else fades, its steady outward push eventually wins and expansion accelerates.

### Precisely
The **cosmological constant** $\Lambda$ is the term Einstein added to the **einstein-field-equations**. Interpreted as dark energy, it is a uniform **vacuum energy density** $\rho_\Lambda = \frac{\Lambda c^2}{8\pi G}$, constant in time, with **equation of state**
$$w \equiv \frac{p}{\rho c^2} = -1.$$
This $w=-1$ — pressure exactly equal to minus the energy density — is the defining signature of a true constant.

### Worked example
Densities dilute as $\rho \propto a^{-3(1+w)}$. For matter ($w=0$): $\rho \propto a^{-3}$. For radiation ($w=1/3$): $\rho \propto a^{-4}$. For $\Lambda$ ($w=-1$): $\rho \propto a^{0} = $ constant. So as $a$ grows, matter and radiation fade while $\Lambda$ holds steady — guaranteeing $\Lambda$ eventually dominates, which is exactly what we observe happening now ($\Omega_\Lambda \approx 0.69$ today).

### Why it's true / how it works
Because $\rho_\Lambda$ is constant, an expanding volume gains energy "for free" — but it does so against the work done by its negative pressure, conserving energy via the **stress-energy** continuity equation $\dot\rho + 3H(\rho + p/c^2) = 0$, which gives $\dot\rho = 0$ precisely when $p = -\rho c^2$.

### Where it connects
$\Lambda$ is the "Λ" of **lambda-cdm** and the leading **dark-energy** candidate. Its constancy ($w=-1$) is what the **dark-energy-equation-of-state** searches test, and its dominance sets the heat-death **cosmic-fate**.

### Watch out
Identifying $\Lambda$ with quantum **vacuum energy** predicts a value $\sim10^{120}$ times too large — the **cosmological constant problem**, perhaps the worst quantitative mismatch in physics. Plus the **coincidence problem**: why are $\Omega_\Lambda$ and $\Omega_m$ comparable *right now*, of all epochs?

atoms.title: ΛCDM — the standard model of cosmology
atoms.summary: A flat universe of ~5% atoms, ~27% cold dark matter, ~68% dark energy fits nearly all cosmological data.

depths.eli5: Cosmology's grand summary is one short recipe for the whole universe: a pinch of ordinary matter (atoms), a big helping of invisible cold dark matter, and an even bigger helping of dark energy, all in a flat universe that got its start from inflation. Remarkably, that single recipe with just a handful of dials explains almost every cosmic observation at once.
depths.core: ΛCDM (say 'Lambda-C-D-M') is the 'standard model of cosmology,' also called the 'concordance model' because many independent datasets agree on it. The name spells out its two key ingredients: Λ (the cosmological constant, i.e. dark energy) and CDM ('cold dark matter' — dark matter that moves slowly, which is what lets fine structure form). It describes a spatially flat universe whose lumps were seeded by inflation's nearly even fluctuations. The mix is roughly 5% ordinary matter, 27% dark matter, and 68% dark energy. With only about six adjustable numbers ('free parameters'), this one model simultaneously fits the CMB, the large-scale galaxy web, Big Bang nucleosynthesis, and supernova distances — an extraordinary feat of economy.
depths.deep: Its economy is its strength: six parameters fit thousands of CMB multipoles and galaxy statistics. Yet it is descriptive, not explanatory — it names dark matter and dark energy without identifying them, and emerging tensions (notably in H₀) probe whether it is complete.

atoms.note: Often called the 'concordance model' because independent data sets agree on its parameters.
atoms.art_prompt: a pie chart of the cosmic energy budget — ~5% atoms, ~27% dark matter, ~68% dark energy — beside a CMB power spectrum fit by a single model curve

quiz.prompt: What are the approximate fractions of ordinary matter, dark matter, and dark energy in ΛCDM?
quiz.answer: About 5% ordinary (baryonic) matter, 27% cold dark matter, and 68% dark energy.

quiz.prompt: Explain why ΛCDM is celebrated yet considered incomplete.
quiz.answer: With only ~six parameters it fits the CMB, structure, BBN, and supernovae together — a huge success — but it merely labels dark matter and dark energy without explaining what they are, and faces tensions like the Hubble tension.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Cosmology's grand summary is one short recipe for the whole universe: a pinch of ordinary atoms, a big helping of invisible cold dark matter, and an even bigger helping of dark energy, in a flat universe seeded by inflation. Remarkably, that single recipe with a handful of dials explains almost every cosmic observation at once.

### Precisely
**ΛCDM** ("Lambda Cold Dark Matter"), the **standard model of cosmology** or **concordance model**, describes a spatially flat universe ($\Omega_k \approx 0$) governed by the **friedmann-equations** with a **cosmological-constant** $\Lambda$ plus **cold** (slow-moving) **dark matter**, with **inflation**-seeded, nearly scale-invariant, Gaussian, adiabatic fluctuations. The present budget is approximately:
$$\Omega_b \approx 0.05,\quad \Omega_c \approx 0.27,\quad \Omega_\Lambda \approx 0.68.$$

### Worked example
The model has only about **six free parameters** (e.g. $\Omega_b h^2$, $\Omega_c h^2$, the optical depth $\tau$, the scalar amplitude $A_s$ and tilt $n_s$, and the acoustic-scale angle $\theta_*$). From those six, it predicts the *entire* CMB **acoustic-peaks** spectrum (thousands of multipoles), the **bbn** abundances, the **baryon-acoustic-oscillations** scale, and the supernova **standard-candles** Hubble diagram — and they all match.

### Why it's true / how it works
ΛCDM's strength is economy: six numbers fit datasets spanning $z \sim 1100$ (the CMB) to $z \sim 0$ (local galaxies), across radiation, matter, and dark-energy eras. The agreement of *independent* probes on the *same* parameters is why it is called the "concordance" model.

### Where it connects
It synthesizes essentially every atom in this branch: **inflation**, **bbn**, **recombination**, **cmb-anisotropies**, **dark-matter-halos**, **large-scale-structure**, and **dark-energy** — the unified picture of **cosmic-history-synthesis**.

### Watch out
ΛCDM is *descriptive, not explanatory*: it names dark matter and dark energy without identifying them. And it faces growing tensions — most prominently the **hubble-tension** (a $\sim5\sigma$ disagreement in $H_0$) and hints of evolving **dark-energy-equation-of-state** — which probe whether the model is complete.

atoms.title: The cosmic distance ladder
atoms.summary: Distances are bootstrapped in rungs — parallax to Cepheids to supernovae — each calibrating the next.

depths.eli5: No single tool can measure every cosmic distance, so astronomers climb a ladder. The bottom rung measures nearby stars directly; that result calibrates a tool good for slightly farther objects; that one calibrates a tool for even farther objects; and so on out to distant galaxies. Each rung leans on the rung beneath it — which is why the whole thing is called a 'ladder.'
depths.core: The 'cosmic distance ladder' is the chain of methods astronomers use to measure ever-greater distances, each one calibrating the next. The bottom rung is 'parallax,' a pure geometry trick: a nearby star appears to shift slightly against the background as Earth orbits the Sun, and the size of that shift gives the distance directly. Parallax distances calibrate Cepheid variable stars; Cepheids (visible in nearby galaxies) in turn calibrate Type Ia supernovae; and supernovae, bright enough to see across the cosmos, reach the far universe. Combine the ladder's distances with the galaxies' redshifts and you get the Hubble constant and the history of cosmic expansion.
depths.deep: Each rung inherits the calibration uncertainty of the rungs below, so systematic errors (e.g., Cepheid metallicity, dust, supernova standardization) propagate up the ladder — which is exactly where the local-distance-ladder value of H₀ might diverge from the early-universe value.

quiz.prompt: Name the three classic rungs of the cosmic distance ladder in order of increasing reach.
quiz.answer: Geometric parallax, Cepheid variable stars, and Type Ia supernovae.

quiz.prompt: Why does a calibration error in one rung threaten the whole ladder?
quiz.answer: Each rung is calibrated by the one below it, so a systematic error propagates upward and biases the final distance and H₀ estimate.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
No single tool measures every cosmic distance, so astronomers climb a ladder. The bottom rung measures nearby stars directly by geometry; that result calibrates a tool good for slightly farther objects; that calibrates a tool for even farther ones; and so on out to distant galaxies. Each rung leans on the one beneath — which is why it is a *ladder*.

### Precisely
The **cosmic distance ladder** is a chain of distance methods, each calibrating the next:
1. **Parallax** — pure geometry: a nearby star shifts by angle $p$ as Earth orbits, giving $d\,[\text{pc}] = 1/p\,[\text{arcsec}]$.
2. **Cepheid variables** — the period–luminosity relation gives $L$, calibrated by parallax.
3. **Type Ia supernovae** — uniform peak brightness, calibrated by Cepheids in host galaxies.
Supernovae reach far enough to measure the **hubble-law** and expansion history.

### Worked example
A star with parallax $p = 0.01''$ lies at $d = 1/0.01 = 100\,\text{pc}$. The Gaia mission measures parallaxes to $\sim10\,\mu\text{as}$, reaching $\sim10\,\text{kpc}$ — far enough to calibrate Milky Way **Cepheids**, which (being $10^3$–$10^4$ times brighter than the Sun) are visible in galaxies tens of Mpc away, where Type Ia **standard-candles** then take over to billions of light-years.

### Why it's true / how it works
Each rung is *anchored* by the rung below: parallax fixes Cepheid luminosities, Cepheids fix supernova luminosities. Combining the ladder's distances with measured redshifts yields $H_0$ — the SH0ES program gets $H_0 \approx 73\,\text{km/s/Mpc}$ this way.

### Where it connects
The ladder anchors the local **hubble-law** and is one side of the **hubble-tension**. Its top rung, Type Ia **standard-candles**, revealed **dark-energy**.

### Watch out
Calibration errors *propagate upward*: a systematic in Cepheid distances (metallicity, crowding, dust) biases every supernova distance above it, and hence $H_0$. This propagation is exactly where the local ladder value of $H_0$ might genuinely diverge from the early-universe CMB value.

atoms.title: Horizons and the observable universe
atoms.summary: Light has only had finite time to reach us, so we see a sphere ~46 billion light-years in comoving radius.

depths.eli5: Light travels fast but not instantly, and the universe is only so old. So we can only see things whose light has had time to reach us since the beginning. That sets an edge to what we can observe — not an edge of the universe itself, just an edge of our view. Beyond it the universe almost certainly keeps going; its light simply hasn't arrived yet.
depths.core: Because the universe has a finite age (about 13.8 billion years), light has only had so long to travel, which creates a 'particle horizon' — the greatest distance from which light could possibly have reached us by now. The 'observable universe' is everything inside that horizon. Its present 'comoving radius' (distance measured in today's stretched-out units) is about 46 billion light-years. That's far bigger than the naive 13.8 billion light-years you'd guess from the age, because space kept expanding while the ancient light was in transit, carrying its sources much farther away. The whole universe is at least this big and probably vastly larger — we just can't see past our horizon.
depths.deep: There is also a cosmological event horizon in an accelerating universe: galaxies beyond a certain comoving distance are receding such that their future light will never reach us, so the observable universe's content (not just its apparent edge) is being slowly cut off as Λ dominates.

atoms.art_prompt: Earth at the center of a translucent sphere of comoving radius ~46 billion light-years, with galaxies fading out at the particle horizon

quiz.prompt: Roughly what is the comoving radius of the observable universe?
quiz.answer: About 46 billion light-years, even though the universe is only ~13.8 billion years old.

quiz.prompt: Why is the observable universe larger than 13.8 billion light-years despite light only traveling for 13.8 billion years?
quiz.answer: Space expanded while the light was in transit, so the regions that emitted ancient light are now much farther away than the distance the light covered.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Light travels fast but not instantly, and the universe is only so old. So we can see only things whose light has had time to reach us since the beginning. That sets an edge to what we can *observe* — not an edge of the universe itself, just an edge of our view. Beyond it the universe almost certainly continues; its light simply has not arrived yet.

### Precisely
Because the universe has finite age ($\approx13.8\,\text{Gyr}$), light has traveled only so far, defining the **particle horizon** — the greatest comoving distance from which light could have reached us. The **observable universe** is everything inside it. Its present **comoving radius** is about **46 billion light-years** ($\approx14\,\text{Gpc}$), making the observable universe roughly $93$ billion light-years across.

### Worked example
Why 46, not 13.8, billion light-years? Because space expanded *while the light traveled*. A photon emitted at **recombination** ($z\approx1100$) traveled for $13.8\,\text{Gyr}$, but its source has since been carried far away by expansion. The comoving particle horizon is $d_p = c\int_0^{t_0} dt/a(t)$, which for ΛCDM evaluates to $\sim46\,\text{Gly}$ — over three times the naive light-travel distance.

### Why it's true / how it works
The integral $\int dt/a$ weights early times (small $a$) heavily, so most of the comoving horizon was accumulated when the universe was young and small. Expansion then stretched those early-emitted regions to their present great distances, producing a horizon much larger than $c\,t_0$.

### Where it connects
The horizon frames what cosmology can ever measure; it caps the reach of the **hubble-law** and the **big-bang** observability. In an accelerating universe (**dark-energy**), there is also a future **event horizon** that limits what we will *ever* see.

### Watch out
The observable universe is *our* view, centered on us — not the whole universe, which is at least this big and probably vastly (possibly infinitely) larger. And distant galaxies receding faster than $c$ are *not* breaking relativity: cosmological recession is space stretching, not motion through space.

atoms.title: Gravitational lensing
atoms.summary: Mass bends light, so foreground masses magnify and distort background galaxies — a direct probe of total mass.

depths.eli5: Just as a glass lens bends light to form an image, a heavy object in space bends the light passing near it. So when a massive galaxy or galaxy cluster sits between us and something farther away, it warps and magnifies the background object's light. By studying exactly how that light gets bent, astronomers can weigh the foreground mass — including mass we can't see at all.
depths.core: General relativity predicts that mass bends the path of light (recall spacetime curvature steering everything that moves, including light). A foreground galaxy or cluster therefore acts as a 'gravitational lens,' producing stretched 'arcs,' multiple copies of a single background source, and overall magnification. The crucial point: lensing responds to ALL mass — whether it shines or not — so it maps the total mass directly, making it one of the best tools for detecting dark matter and measuring the geometry of the universe. 'Strong lensing' gives dramatic, obvious arcs and even complete 'Einstein rings'; 'weak lensing' is far subtler, a roughly 1% systematic warping of the shapes of millions of galaxies ('cosmic shear') that only shows up statistically.
depths.deep: Strong lensing makes dramatic arcs and Einstein rings; weak lensing measures subtle ~1% shape distortions of millions of galaxies statistically ('cosmic shear'), probing the growth of structure and constraining the matter density and dark energy independently of galaxy bias.

atoms.note: First confirmed in 1919 (light bending by the Sun during a solar eclipse) — an early triumph of general relativity.
sources: NASA/ESA public education materials (Hubble lensing images)
atoms.art_prompt: a foreground galaxy cluster bending background galaxies into bright arcs and an Einstein ring, with a faint total-mass contour map overlaid

quiz.prompt: What does gravitational lensing respond to that makes it valuable for dark matter studies?
quiz.answer: Total mass — both luminous and dark — so it maps mass directly regardless of whether it emits light.

quiz.prompt: Distinguish strong from weak gravitational lensing.
quiz.answer: Strong lensing produces visible arcs, multiple images, and Einstein rings; weak lensing produces tiny statistical shape distortions ('cosmic shear') measured over many galaxies.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Just as a glass lens bends light to form an image, a heavy object in space bends light passing near it. So when a massive galaxy or cluster sits between us and something farther, it warps and magnifies the background object's light. By studying exactly how the light bends, astronomers can weigh the foreground mass — including mass we cannot see at all.

### Precisely
General relativity (**spacetime-curvature**) predicts mass deflects light. A point mass $M$ deflects a ray with impact parameter $b$ by
$$\hat\alpha = \frac{4GM}{c^2 b},$$
twice the Newtonian prediction. A foreground **lens** (galaxy or cluster) produces magnified, distorted, or multiple images. **Strong lensing** gives dramatic arcs, multiple images, and complete **Einstein rings**; **weak lensing** produces subtle $\sim1\%$ statistical shape distortions ("cosmic shear") across millions of galaxies.

### Worked example
The Sun's deflection of grazing starlight: $b = R_\odot = 6.96\times10^{8}\,\text{m}$, $M_\odot = 2.0\times10^{30}\,\text{kg}$, so
$$\hat\alpha = \frac{4(6.67\times10^{-11})(2.0\times10^{30})}{(3\times10^8)^2(6.96\times10^8)} \approx 8.5\times10^{-6}\,\text{rad} \approx 1.75''.$$
Eddington's 1919 eclipse expedition measured exactly this — an early triumph of general relativity.

### Why it's true / how it works
Light follows null **geodesics** through curved spacetime; near mass, those geodesics bend. Crucially, lensing responds to *all* mass — luminous or dark — so it maps the **total** gravitating mass directly, making it one of the best **dark-matter** probes and a clean geometric tool.

### Where it connects
Lensing weighs **dark-matter-halos**, provides decisive **dark-matter-evidence** (the Bullet Cluster), and — via weak-lensing cosmic shear — constrains the matter density and **dark-energy-equation-of-state** independently of galaxy bias.

### Watch out
The GR deflection is *twice* the naive Newtonian "falling photon" value — the factor of 2 comes from the curvature of *space* as well as time, and getting it right was a key test. Weak lensing's $\sim1\%$ signal is buried under galaxies' intrinsic shapes, so it only emerges *statistically* over huge samples.

atoms.title: The Hubble tension
atoms.summary: Local and early-universe measurements of H₀ disagree at ~5σ — possibly a crack in ΛCDM.

depths.eli5: Two trustworthy methods both try to measure how fast the universe is expanding today, and they keep getting different answers. The gap is now too big to blame on bad luck or sloppy measuring. So either there's a subtle mistake nobody has spotted, or our theory of the universe is missing something. This unsolved disagreement is the 'Hubble tension.'
depths.core: Both numbers are values of the Hubble constant H₀, the expansion rate today. The 'distance-ladder' method (climb parallax → Cepheids → Type Ia supernovae, as in the SH0ES project) measures the nearby universe directly and gets H₀ ≈ 73 km/s/Mpc. The 'early-universe' method instead reads H₀ off the Planck satellite's CMB map by assuming the ΛCDM model, and gets ≈ 67.4 km/s/Mpc. The gap between them is about '5σ' — '5 sigma' means five times the size of the expected measurement scatter, a level physicists treat as far too large to be random chance. So this is a real puzzle: it points to either an undiscovered measurement error ('systematic') or a genuine gap in ΛCDM.
depths.deep: Independent BAO+BBN inferences cluster near the low (Planck) value, sharpening the puzzle; proposed fixes like early dark energy modify the sound horizon before recombination, but no single model yet resolves H₀ without worsening other data — the tension remains genuinely open.

atoms.note: Planck (early-universe) ≈ 67.4 ± 0.5; SH0ES (local) ≈ 73.0 ± 1.0 km/s/Mpc.
sources: arXiv astro-ph (Hubble tension reviews, SH0ES, Planck)
